papers.title: Quantitative Ultrasound Characterizes Perfusion Trajectories in Healthy and Inflamed Gingival Wound Healing
papers.summary: Rationale and Objectives: Visual examination of extraction-site healing provides limited insight into underlying vascular recovery. We developed a quantitative ultrasound framework to assess gingival perfusion and persistent inflammation. Materials and Methods: Patients (n = 51) undergoing extraction and socket preservation were imaged longitudinally using color-flow ultrasound and laser speckle contrast analysis (LASCA) from 2 weeks to 3 months after extraction. Pre-scan-converted Total Recall Imaging (TRI) data with phase information were processed using scan conversion, bilateral filtering, and power estimation to derive velocity-weighted color pixel density (CPDvel). Gingival regions of interest were automatically segmented using deep learning and assessed with Dice and Bland-Altman analyses. CPDvel was compared between healthy and inflamed visits in early (35 days) periods and with LASCA. Results: Segmentation achieved a mean Dice score of 0.98 and median of 0.99 (IQR, 0.98-0.99), with minimal area bias (-0.005%; 95% limits of agreement, -1.68% to 1.67%). Median CPDvel decreased by 81% between early and recovery periods in healthy visits (p = 0.01), compared with a nonsignificant 26% reduction in inflamed visits (p = 0.31). During recovery, CPDvel was higher in inflamed than healthy visits (0.12 vs 0.03 cm/s; p = 0.04). LASCA showed smaller reductions (13% and 9%, respectively). CPDvel was positively correlated with LASCA in healthy (one-sided p = 0.03) and inflamed visits (one-sided p = 0.13). Conclusions: TRI-based quantitative ultrasound enabled automated perfusion assessment with reduced dependence on scanner display settings. Distinct perfusion patterns and more pronounced temporal changes than LASCA support its potential for noninvasive monitoring of oral wound healing and persistent inflammation.

papers.title: The Role of Electron-Nuclear Coupling on Chemical and Physical Processes
papers.summary: Over the last few decades, Born-Oppenheimer (BO) and Born-Oppenheimer-Huang (BOH) treatments for electron-nuclear equation of motion have been considered as the cornerstone for qualitative as well as quantitative exploration and understanding of chemical and physical processes. The BO approximation due to the large mass difference between electrons and nuclei as well as the energy separation among the electronic states could able to predict some of the processes (chemical and physical) satisfactorily at lower energy regime. Such approximation (BO) quite often fails for those cases with the involvement of excited electronic states, in particular, due to the coupling among the states. On the other hand, the BO treatment provides two important quantities, namely, the adiabatic potential energy surfaces (PESs) and the nonadiabatic coupling terms (NACTs) determining the forces, which control the motion of the nuclei in a molecule. The NACTs play a major role in photoexcitation spectra, charge transfer chemical reactions, ferroelectric property and other processes, where significant anomalies are observed between single and multiple PES(s) results. Since the NACTs often exhibit singularity at the close vicinity of degenerate states forming conical intersections (CIs), such coupling terms could break the symmetry of the molecular processes changing the observables qualitatively.

papers.title: Estimating Irving-Kirkwood pressure profiles from per-atom virial and density profiles: a closure for the contour-dependent term in planar liquid films
papers.summary: The local pressure tensor of an inhomogeneous fluid is not unique. Two tangential profiles are in common use in planar simulations: the Irving-Kirkwood (IK) profile, which requires a dedicated pass over every pair of atoms for every slab, and the per-atom virial (PAV) profile, which molecular-dynamics codes produce at negligible cost and coincides with the Harasima contour. The two differ by the derivative of a pair quantity, P_T^IK - P_T^PAV = dQ/dz. We show that, for Lennard-Jones free-standing films, Q(z) can be predicted from the density profile and the bulk radial distribution function of the coexisting liquid: under the closure rho2(r1,r2) ~ rho(z1) rho(z2) g(r12), with a pair-local interpolation of g between its liquid and dilute limits, Q is a double integral of rho(z) against a kernel built from u'(r) g(r). The estimator P_T^IK,est = P_T^PAV + dQ/dz is tested against IK profiles measured on the same trajectories for 20 films (thicknesses 7-25 sigma, three cutoff radii, two temperatures): the root-mean-square residual is 0.001-0.002 epsilon/sigma^3, against 0.010-0.021 for the uncorrected profile, and Q, the amount that the contour choice transfers between the two interfaces of a film with non-equivalent surfaces, is recovered to within 0.6% of the surface tension. Applied to the normal component, the same closure removes 83-92% of the spurious structure of the per-atom zz profile, a test that needs no IK run. Its mixture form is validated on three two-component films with an adsorbate unequally distributed between their faces, where it resolves the tension of each face; a clean face recovers the tension of the pure film.

papers.title: Laboratory study of mineral dust optical properties extending in the far-infrared spectral range
papers.summary: Mineral dust is one of the most abundant atmospheric aerosol types and remains a major source of uncertainty in estimates of aerosol radiative forcing. This uncertainty is particularly important in the far-infrared (FIR) spectral region, where the optical properties of natural mineral dust, especially its complex refractive index (CRI), remain poorly known. Previous measurements have commonly relied on pellet- or film-based methods, which can alter particle size, shape, and vibrational modes, inducing errors in the CRI determination. In this study, we present a laboratory investigation on six natural mineral dust samples with contrasting compositions and originated from major dust source regions worldwide, including Arizona, Atacama, China, Niger, Saudi Arabia, and Tunisia. Suspended dust aerosols were generated under controlled dry conditions and characterized using extinction spectroscopy from the infrared 250 to 4000 cm^-1 (2.5 to 40 micrometers) to the Ultraviolet-Visible (UV-Vis) from 10000 to 40000 cm^-1 (0.25 to 1 micrometer) spectral range, combined with particle size distribution measurements. The real and imaginary parts of the CRI were retrieved for all six samples, revealing a significant absorption and pronounced spectral variability in the FIR. These variations should be accounted for in remote sensing and dust radiative effect studies.

papers.title: Focusing through coupled multimode fibers for miniaturized single-atom tweezer arrays
papers.summary: Real-world deployment of quantum technologies requires systems in low SWaP-C packages. Quantum platforms based on ultracold atoms typically trap and control atoms with optical tweezers using light focused through bulky objective lenses, which are costly and sensitive to misalignment. Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a compact route to focusing light, but their use in forming optical tweezers for cold atoms has been limited to a single fiber. Here we use a 2x1 MMF fused coupler to obtain two independent control paths sharing a common distal facet. We form near-diffraction-limited tweezers through each channel, suppress interference by applying a small frequency offset between the channels, and demonstrate that the tweezer separation is insensitive to misalignment of the input coupling. This work provides a route to reconfigurable single-atom arrays in low SWaP-C environments.

papers.title: Second-order Bethe-Salpeter kernels: the interplay of vertex-corrected quasiparticle energies and the screened interaction
papers.summary: We study second-order Bethe-Salpeter kernels generated by truncating an iterative formulation of Hedin's equations after the second cycle. Starting from the Hartree-Fock or the $GW$ self-energy, whose first cycles correspond to TDHF and $GW$+BSE, we obtain the second-cycle kernel by differentiating the first-cycle correlation self-energy with the interacting correlation function replaced by the non-interacting one, and evaluate it in the static limit of the effective kernel. Using fixed restricted Hartree-Fock orbitals, we benchmark 30 singlet and 28 triplet excitation energies for seven small molecules (six for the triplets) against the theoretical best estimates from QUEST v1.2. The second cycle lowers the mean absolute error (MAE) in both sequences. For the $GW$ sequence, the MAE decreases from 0.63 to 0.29 eV (singlets), on par with ADC(2) (0.30 eV), and from 0.43 to 0.38 eV (triplets). BSE$^{(2)}$@HF removes the triplet instabilities of TDHF and yields MAEs of 0.43 and 0.38 eV, or 0.31 and 0.30 eV when the Tamm-Dancoff approximation is applied in all cycles. Assigning the statically screened interaction $W_0$ to the exchange part of the $GW$ self-energy counts second-order screening twice in the second-cycle kernel and strongly blueshifts valence excitations. Without this double counting, dressing the exchange-type terms with $W_0$ lowers the singlet MAE from 0.37 to 0.29 eV but leaves the triplets nearly unchanged. Replacing second-order Green's function (GF2) quasiparticle energies by vertex-corrected ones in the same kernel raises excitation energies by about 0.7 eV, improving Rydberg but degrading valence excitations. A perturbative dynamical correction of the kernel blueshifts valence excitations by 0.3-0.4 eV and increases the errors of all full-matrix BSE$^{(2)}$ variants. The consistent improvement over the first cycle suggests that higher cycles are worth pursuing.

papers.title: Penetration of a sphere in a pool: Secondary pinch-off
papers.summary: The water entry of solid bodies, in particular spheres, has been the subject of numerous studies due to its relevance in multiple applications, especially focusing on cavity dynamics and the resulting forces and subsequent trajectories. The role of wettability in cavity formation and sustainability has been experimentally and theoretically addressed in the past; however, typically only up to the occurrence of a primary air cavity pinch-off. What is less explored is how wettability can influence higher-order pinch-offs. In the following study, especially secondary pinch-offs are shown to determine whether a sphere trajectory is terminally ascending, i.e., the sphere returns to the surface, or terminally descending: wettability is shown to be a strong influencing factor. This study begins with a series of systematic experiments, comparing the entry and trajectory of spheres over a range of impact Reynolds and Froude numbers, but also with varying surface wettability. From time resolved trajectories, a force balance is computed, illustrating the role of buoyancy, arising from the volume of any sustained air cavity in the wake of the sphere. Secondary pinch-offs alter this volume; hence, the terminal trajectory. A force-scale comparison and local radial balance at the cavity neck are then presented, suggesting how wettability influences the secondary pinch-off.

papers.title: Turbulence on Hybrid Lattices: regular grids meet self similar cascade models
papers.summary: Turbulent cascades in high Reynolds number regimes span many decades in scale, which can be challenging for numerical simulations. Cascade models that use logarithmic discretization can help, but these have limited capabilities to describe spatial structures or real space details. Hybrid Lattices (HLs) are proposed in order to provide a novel framework to investigate turbulent cascades in Fourier space, combining regular grids and cascade models based on logarithmic discretisations. The approach consists of a regular spectral region, capable of resolving large scale coherent structures, that is extended in a recurrent, asymptotically self similar fashion, spanning many decades in scale. The idea comes from shell models and their extensions, namely the logarithmic lattices, the nested polyhedra models or the spiral chain models. The logarithmic spacing factor of those models, such as the golden ratio, typically prevents interactions between a regular grid and a self similar model. HLs are constructed by expanding a regular region in Fourier space through recurrence relations (e.g. the Fibonacci recurrence relation), generating an asymptotically logarithmic lattice where Cartesian components remain integer multiples of the regular Fourier space grid spacing. This way, the resulting grid preserves triadic interactions linking regular and recurrent regions, allowing energy transfer across these different regions. However, the sharp reduction in triads connecting the two regions creates a bottleneck effect, and in order to address this issue, a region of ghost points at the boundary had to be introduced, efficiently allowing the flux to leak into the recurrent part. The HL framework is then tested for the one dimensional Burgers equation, and for two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes turbulence.

papers.title: Novel Mixed Approximate Deconvolution Large-Eddy Simulation Models for Two-Phase Flows
papers.summary: Approximate Deconvolution (AD) frameworks for Large-Eddy Simulation (LES) offer a promising approach for modeling multiscale interactions in turbulent multiphase flows. However, some conventional formulations exhibit structural inconsistencies, identified in our previous work [Amani E., Molaei M.B., Ghorbani M. 2024 Novel mixed approximate deconvolution subgrid-scale models for large-eddy simulation. Physics of Fluids 36] which can impact the accuracy and robustness of AD-LES. To address this issue, the present study extends a family of structurally consistent AD closures to turbulent two-phase flows. Specifically, we introduce the Alternative Local Dynamic Model with Kinetic energy equation (A-LDMK), an improved non-equilibrium one-equation mixed eddy-viscosity AD framework. These closures are evaluated through a posteriori analyses of a single-phase turbulent channel flow and a turbulent two-phase gas-liquid mixing layer. The results indicate that the consistent frameworks enhance numerical stability and can sustain energy backscatter under less restrictive stability constraints compared to standard dynamic procedures. Specifically, the proposed A-LDMK provides the most accurate prediction of the multiscale primary atomization cascade in terms of droplet size distribution, compared to the other assessed closures.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Latent Neural ODEs for Reduced-Order Modeling of Hydrogen, Ammonia, and Methane Combustion Kinetics
papers.summary: Detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms are computationally expensive in reacting-flow simulations because of their high dimensionality and numerical stiffness. We develop an end-to-end physics-informed autoencoder neural ordinary differential equation (PI-AE-NODE) framework in which an encoder compresses the thermochemical state into a low-dimensional latent space, a Neural ODE advances it continuously in time, and a decoder reconstructs the temperature and all species mass fractions. Elemental conservation, mass conservation, and enthalpy consistency are embedded in the training objective. The framework is applied to H$_2$/air, NH$_3$/air, and CH$_4$/air autoignition using detailed mechanisms of increasing size and complexity, which are represented accurately with only a few latent variables. Compared with an otherwise identical data-driven model, the physical constraints improve ignition delay prediction and conservation behaviour. The models reproduce major and intermediate species evolution at both training and unseen conditions, and their latent dynamics permit efficient explicit integration, with the computational advantage over the detailed mechanisms increasing with mechanism size.

papers.title: A Momentum-weighted Interface Stabilization Approach for Fluid-Structure Interaction with Strong Added-Mass Effects
papers.summary: Partitioned fluid-structure interaction (FSI) schemes permit the reuse of optimized standalone solvers but can become unstable under strong fluid added-mass effects, particularly when structural inertia is small relative to fluid inertia. This work traces the instability to the discrepancy between the interface pressure Schur complements of the monolithic and Dirichlet- Neumann partitioned systems, as revealed by a fixed-point analysis of the linearized FSI problem. Motivated by this analysis, a momentum-weighted interface stabilization (MWIS) is proposed, in which the interface pressure block of the fluid subproblem is augmented by an operator constructed from the fluid and structural interface momentum operators. The augmentation is consistent by construction, vanishing at convergence so that the monolithic solution is recovered. A sparse diagonal approximation of the operator, derived from element metrics, limits intersolver data exchange to quantities comparable in size to standard interface coupling data while requiring minimal modifications to the standalone solvers. Numerical experiments, spanning a linear model and established nonlinear FSI benchmarks, demonstrate improved coupling robustness in regimes of strong added-mass where the standard Dirichlet-Neumann scheme diverges.

papers.title: Soft X-Ray Detection Down to the Nitrogen K-Edge Using a Pixelated iLGAD Sensor
papers.summary: Hybrid pixel detectors represent the state-of-the-art technology for hard X-ray experiments at synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers, owing to their high frame rates, extended dynamic range, and scalable detection areas. However, their application in the soft X-ray regime remains bottlenecked by the challenge of developing a sensor that can achieve high quantum efficiency and an sufficient signal-to-noise ratio at low photon energies. Here, we present inverse low-gain avalanche diode (iLGAD) sensors integrated with a thin entrance window, demonstrating single-photon resolution down to 390 eV (below the Nitrogen K-edge) with a signal-to-noise ratio of 5. Two gain layer designs, standard gain layer and shallow gain layer, were systematically investigated to evaluate their spectral response as a function of photon energy and operating temperature. A double-peak feature is observed in the energy spectrum, arising from the dependence of charge multiplication on photon absorption depth. Furthermore, a phenomenological spectral fitting model was established, enabling the quantitative extraction of the effective $\mathrm{n}^+$ layer thickness and gain layer depth. Beyond providing a fundamental understanding of iLGAD charge multiplication mechanisms and characterization results in the soft X-ray regime, these findings lay the foundation for developing large-area, high-frame-rate hybrid pixel detectors for soft X-ray. This advancement directly benefits soft X-ray photon science applications, including high-resolution ptychography, spectroscopy, and resonant scattering at synchrotron and FEL beamlines.

papers.title: Onset of Radiatively Driven Convection in Ice-Covered Freshwater Lakes
papers.summary: This work investigates the formation and growth of Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities (RTIs) during the onset of radiatively driven convection (RDC) in seasonally ice-covered freshwater lakes. Two-dimensional direct numerical simulations (DNS) and linear analysis allow for the investigation of how environmental factors, including thermal stratification, water clarity, and solar forcing influence RTI formation. It is found that for strongly stratified lakes, there is a period of dormancy before the water column forms a gravitationally unstable layer that allows RTI growth. Conversely, for weakly stratified lakes the water column can become unstable almost immediately, allowing for rapid RTI growth. A linear analysis is performed to investigate the early RTI growth dynamics, and its results compare well with DNS. Notably, the wavelengths and depths of RTIs, and their associated time-dependent growth rates, are all captured by the linearised dynamics. Predictions of RDC onset obtained using the linear model show good agreement with DNS results. When the analysis is applied to field measurements of ice-covered lakes, it is found that weakly stratified lakes may take a few hours before RDC onset whereas strongly stratified lakes may not see RDC onset after a full day of clear-sky spring conditions.

papers.title: Field-resolved observation and quantification of the instantaneous Kerr response in semiconductors
papers.summary: The optical Kerr effect, whereby the refractive index of a material changes with light intensity, underpins nonlinear photonics and emerging mid-infrared technologies. Accurate determination of the nonlinear refractive index is therefore essential, yet conventional intensity-based techniques infer the nonlinear phase shift indirectly from changes in beam propagation or optical spectra. Moreover, methods such as the $z$-scan cannot resolve the temporal evolution of the nonlinear response, making it difficult to distinguish instantaneous Kerr nonlinearities from delayed contributions, including free-carrier effects. Here, we investigate the nonlinear optical response of germanium at $5 \mu\mathrm{m}$ using field-resolved degenerate pump-probe spectroscopy. By measuring the transmitted probe electric field as a function of pump-probe delay, we directly retrieve the pump-induced phase shift and its temporal evolution while retaining sensitivity to changes in absorption. We observe cross-phase modulation that follows the pump intensity envelope and vanishes when the pump and probe no longer overlap, consistent with an instantaneous Kerr response. The phase shift scales linearly with pump intensity, yielding a nonlinear refractive index of $n_2=(0.87\pm0.16)\times10^{-17} \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{W}$. Our results establish the instantaneous Kerr effect as the dominant contribution to the measured nonlinear phase shift under our experimental conditions and demonstrate field-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy as a direct, time-resolved method for determining the nonlinear refractive index and distinguishing instantaneous from delayed optical responses.

papers.title: Magnetic Johnson noise from arbitrarily shaped conductors: experimental validation of the fluctuation-dissipation finite-element method
papers.summary: Magnetic Johnson noise--magnetic noise caused by thermal current fluctuations in conducting materials--can interfere with measurements and limit their sensitivity. As the sensitivity of experiments increases, it becomes increasingly important to accurately estimate the magnetic Johnson noise from experimental components with complex shapes during both the design and analysis phases. A particularly powerful approach is to combine the fluctuation-dissipation theorem with finite-element calculations. This versatile approach can be used to calculate the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors of arbitrary geometry for a wide range of frequencies and for magnetic field detectors with general geometries, such as a finite-sized loop or a gradiometer. Using a SQUID gradiometer array, we measured the magnetic Johnson noise from conductors with complex geometries and compared the results with calculations performed using this method. The calculations reproduce both the measured noise amplitude and its frequency dependence, providing an experimental validation of this method. We also performed a detailed analysis of how the geometry and material parameters affect the frequency dependence of magnetic Johnson noise.

papers.title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
papers.summary: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.

papers.title: High efficiency superconducting filterbank with impedance-defined resolution for millimeter-wave spectroscopy
papers.summary: We present a high efficiency, moderate resolution on-chip superconducting filterbank spectrometer designed for line intensity mapping and broadband wave-like dark matter searches. Existing implementations used by the millimeter-wave community rely on resistive feedline termination for standing wave mitigation which caps the per-channel efficiency $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ at 50\% and utilize microstrip resonators which highly couple the resolving power $\mathcal{R}=\nu/\delta\nu$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ to thin-film dielectric loss. The architecture presented in this paper addresses these limitations by eliminating the termination resistor and employing niobium coplanar waveguide resonators patterned directly on single-crystal silicon, which fixes the resonator's internal quality factor by the silicon substrate property rather than by the loss tangent of a deposited film. The resolving power is set by the impedance ratio between the resonator and feedline. Electromagnetic and circuit simulations of a ten-channel filterbank near 90~GHz at unity oversampling show $\mathcal{R}=1170$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}> 78\%$, with no significant trend in efficiency across channels. A ten-channel prototype, designed for $\mathcal{R}=92\pm5$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}=(81\pm3)\%$ over 90--106~GHz with a 560~nm interlayer based on simulations, was fabricated and optically characterized, yielding $\mathcal{R}=208\pm74$ and $\eta_\mathrm{ch}=(77\pm6)\%$. Measured $\eta_\mathrm{ch}$ well above the 50\% termination limit, together with demonstrated impedance tuning of $\mathcal{R}$, validate the design principles of this filterbank spectrometer and establishes a route to high-efficiency, high-resolution on-chip spectrometer arrays.

papers.title: Gapless and Non-Equilibrium Topology in Blockaded Ladders
papers.summary: We propose a multi-leg PXYP model as a minimal setting to explore constraint-induced intertwinement between itinerant and internal degrees of freedom. We argue that the Rydberg-like blockade induces correlations in squeezed space, providing a unified mechanism for nontrivial string order both in and out of equilibrium. In a two-leg geometry, this leads to an intrinsically gapless topological ground state, which can terminate at a supersymmetric multicritical point. This mechanism also leads to the preservation of string order for parametrically long times after a quench, which we verify using tensor network simulations and a classical stochastic approximation to the dynamics. In a three-leg geometry, the blockade leads to an additional emergent $U(1)$ symmetry, resulting in a multicomponent Luttinger liquid where both itinerant and internal degrees of freedom are critical. This family of models arises naturally in a range of quantum simulator platforms such as Rydberg tweezer arrays and dipolar atoms in optical lattices.

papers.title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.summary: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.

papers.title: Subsonic terahertz plasmon instability in space-time plasmonic crystals
papers.summary: We investigate collective plasma-wave dynamics in a two-dimensional electron fluid subected to a travelling periodic modulation of the effective plasma velocity. Using a hydrodynamic description combined with Floquet-Bloch theory, we show that the travelling modulation acts as a moving plasmonic crystal whose band structure is governed by an effective drift velocity in the comoving frame. We demonstrate that the closure of the Bragg gap at the edge of the Brillouin zone gives rise to an exceptional point and triggers a Krein-type instability through the coupling of positive- and negative-energy modes. Analytical expressions are derived for the instability threshold and growth rate, revealing that self-amplification can occur even when the electron drift remains subsonic in the laboratory frame. Numerical simulations of the nonlinear hydrodynamic equations confirm the theoretical predictions and show the evolution towards a saturated regime dominated by a coherent Floquet-Bloch mode. These results identify travelling plasmonic crystals as a novel platform for wave amplification and non-Hermitian band dynamics in electronic fluids.

papers.title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
papers.summary: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

papers.title: Nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic model for the stress-strain and stress-relaxation in metallic glass
papers.summary: We develop a nonlinear visco-elasto-plastic (VEP) model for the stress-strain response of metallic glasses by connecting the deformation dynamics with the material relaxation time obtained from independent stress-relaxation measurements. The material is modeled as a Maxwell-type element, with a nonlinear elastic spring and a stretched-exponential dashpot whose behavior is determined from the separate stress-relaxation data. The model captures the effects of temperature and strain rate on the initial elastic response, stress overshoot, post-yield softening, and steady flow. We independently determine the reference material-time function $X_0(\varepsilon)$ from the stress-relaxation response and the nonlinear material-time variable $X(\varepsilon)$ from the elastic-viscoplastic strain decomposition based on the stress-strain response. We introduce an Eyring-type function or material-time ratio $\phi(\varepsilon)=X(\varepsilon)/X_0(\varepsilon)$ which quantifies the change of relaxation dynamics during nonlinear deformation. Our model provides a simple connection between structural relaxation and yielding in metallic glasses.

papers.title: Exact Electron Dynamics in Linear and Chiral Cavities: Complete Field versus Single-Helicity Reduction
papers.summary: Can a chiral cavity turn a free electron into a Landau-like orbiting particle? We answer with exact solutions of three quadratic electron--cavity models in the dipole limit, valid at arbitrary coupling. A single linearly polarized mode dresses the electron mass, which delays its flight, slows the spreading of a wavepacket and entangles the packet with the cavity. The complete transverse field, with both circular helicities, keeps two commuting, gapless translations at any coupling, mode number and helicity splitting, so the electron stays ballistic and no synthetic magnetic field appears. Keeping a single helicity gives two inequivalent models that are not related by a gauge transformation: reducing before the Power--Zienau--Woolley transformation gives ballistic motion, whereas reducing after it gives a Landau-like crossed-quadrature Hamiltonian. They differ by a real uniform field $B=s\lambda^2/(2\omega_c)$ ($\omega_c$ the mode frequency, $\lambda$ the coupling, $s=\pm1$ the helicity). In the complete theory the frequency $\omega_{-s}$ of the partner helicity, measured against $g^2=\lambda^2/(2\omega_c)$, decides between them: the electron is ballistic for a stiff partner, and Landau-like only at the soft-partner point, through an exact canonical reorganization that holds for the active sector but not for observables such as the electron--photon entanglement. Projecting onto one helicity after the PZW transformation is therefore not by itself a mechanism for synthetic magnetism; the mode content of the cavity is.

papers.title: Chirality inversion and odd transport in a suspension of living rotors
papers.summary: Chiral symmetry breaking is a defining feature of life, visible at all scales from molecules to organisms. Yet how microscopic chirality propagates to shape the macroscopic properties of living matter remains poorly understood. Here, using a new experimental system of spinning microalgae, we show that a living chiral fluid behaves fundamentally differently from an externally driven one. As their density increases, cells self-assemble hydrodynamically into small rotating clusters which merge into a percolating chiral fluid. Strikingly, microscopic and macroscopic vorticity have opposite signs: individual cells all spin clockwise, yet clusters orbit counterclockwise. Combining experiments, theory and simulations, we show that both chirality inversion and percolation are direct consequences of the cells' internally driven nature. We then show how percolation reshapes transport, with even and odd diffusivities responding differently to the emerging network topology.

papers.title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
papers.summary: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.

papers.title: The spin-transfer inverse Faraday effect in Au/YIG thin film bilayers
papers.summary: The inverse Faraday effect (IFE) (the generation of an effective magnetic field in a material upon irradiation with circularly polarized light) offers a pathway to ultrafast, non-thermal control of spin dynamics. In metallic/ferromagnetic-insulator (NM/FMI) bilayers, IFE-driven spin polarization in the metallic layer can be an alternative to generate magnon excitations in the magnetic insulator which otherwise would be inaccessible with photon energies below the insulator bandgap, but this avenue has remained mostly unexplored. In this work, we investigate the regime of spin-transfer via IFE in Au/YIG bilayers, by means of ultrafast time-resolved magneto-optical experiments. Understanding the mechanism of this spin-transfer IFE in these NM/FMI heterostructures is crucial for several reasons: it elucidates the fundamental coupling between light's angular momentum and collective spin modes at buried interfaces, it enables all-optical generation and manipulation of pure spin currents, and it paves the way toward THz-frequency spintronic devices leveraging the insulator's long magnon lifetimes.

We currently lack statistically relevant WVR correction data to understand their expected performance for the ngVLA sites. We also discuss parallel additional approaches alternative and/or complementary to the CWVRs. A path involving tests to establish the functionality, stability, sensitivity, and switched power cal/data synchronism of the CWVR system in the lab and on antenna, followed by on-sky tests, and a parallel effort to assess the utility of autocorrelation outputs of the VLA K-band receivers for delay estimation is recommended. papers.title: Minimal model of sticky collisions in modulated optical traps
papers.summary: Collisional loss of ultracold bialkali molecules is predicted to occur through photo-excitation of collision complexes. We demonstrate that quantum reflection from the long-range potential fundamentally alters loss dynamics, removing the tension between recent experiments and predicted sticking times. This framework provides new testable predictions such as a strong dependence on collision energy, initial molecular state, and long-range interactions, that are absent in the currently used phenomenological model.

papers.title: Spectral Information Content of Diffraction-Limited Images
papers.summary: High-resolution optical imaging is fundamentally limited by diffraction, which imprints wavelength-dependent structure onto the point spread function (PSF) of the optical system. This intrinsic chromaticity implies that in addition to spatial structure, images encode spectral information. We develop the theory of this spectral information content and provide strategies for its optimal extraction with calculations of Fisher information. We show that polychromatic PSF formation can be expressed as a convolution in logarithmic coordinates and define the corresponding spectral transfer function. We derive this function for the Airy disk and find algebraic decay in spectral log-frequency, implying the existence of arbitrarily fine spectral structure in the ideal, noiseless PSF. We use a differentiable forward model to numerically construct the spectral information eigenbasis and quantify the spectroscopic capability of diffraction-limited imaging across a range of noise and detector systematics. We demonstrate injection and recovery of the constrained spectral modes in a realistic simulated example and compare these results with previously reported methods. Our information-theoretic framework provides a generalisable method for spectral characterisation of PSFs spanning a variety of imaging contexts.

papers.title: Transmission and filtering of stochastic rhythms in bursty gene expression
papers.summary: How stochastic rhythms in upstream regulatory signals are transmitted to downstream gene expression is a fundamental question in systems biology. Although experiments have shown that molecular degradation strongly influences downstream rhythmic responses, a general quantitative theory explaining how degradation, stochastic bursting, and upstream timing variability jointly govern rhythm transmission remains lacking. Here we develop a general analytical framework based on a martingale-based orthogonal decomposition, applicable to arbitrarily complex upstream dynamics, including memory effects. We derive exact autocorrelation and power-spectrum transmission laws, establish an oscillation-efficiency contraction principle, and identify a critical degradation rate that provides a necessary and sufficient condition for stochastic rhythm transmission. An explicit rhythm-transmission relation reveals that increasing burst frequency and modulation depth promotes rhythm transmission, whereas greater variability in upstream cycle duration suppresses it. In particular, increasing burst size leaves oscillation efficiency unchanged. The predicted degradation threshold correctly separates all ten pulsing and nonpulsing p53 target proteins reported in previous experiments. These results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how cells selectively preserve or integrate rhythmic regulatory signals.

papers.title: Spectroscopic observations of periodic bursty ejections during a dome-spire-shaped jet
papers.summary: Context: The study investigates the complexity of the formation and evolution of a dome-spire-shaped jet (or anemone jet) that originated in an active region and was presumably driven by null-point magnetic reconnection. Aims: We aim to provide a quantitative estimation of multi-temperature plasma dynamics and physical parameters of the jet and its blob-like features, together with its temporal evolution in three-dimensional perspective. Methods: For this, we analyze unique sit-and-stare spectral (Si IV, Mg II k, and C II) and slit-jaw imaging 1400 {\AA} and 2796 {\AA} observations obtained with the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), with a slit uniquely positioned just above the assumed reconnection site. Co-observations taken with the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph of the Goode Solar Telescope in the chromospheric H$\alpha$ and Ca II 8542.10 {\AA} lines were also analyzed. These data are complemented by EUV imaging information from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory. Results: The IRIS observations reveal that the jet is formed by multiple periodic ($\sim$30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each associated with strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 {\AA} transition-region emission reaching about $-300$ km/s. More importantly, the ejections are grouped into well-defined packets, each lasting approximately 3--5 min. In contrast, only a single Doppler component is observed in the chromospheric Ca II line. Multi-Gaussian decomposition of the Si IV line profiles reveals a highly accelerated plasma, with line-of-sight speed toward the observer increasing linearly from $\sim$30 to 112 km/s over 66 s, corresponding to an acceleration of 1.3 km/s$^2$. The kinetic energy release rate is estimated in the range of $\sim$1.0$\times10^{24}$--1.0$\times10^{25}$ erg\,s$^{-1}$.

papers.title: Relative Influence of Coronal Properties of CME in their Evolution and Geo-effectiveness
papers.summary: Uncertainties in the coronal mass ejection (CME) properties near the Sun remain a major challenge for accurate space weather forecasting. Understanding the sensitivity of CME evolution to the initial parameters is therefore essential for improving the predictions. We investigate the influence of physical CME properties prescribed at 0.1 AU on their subsequent heliospheric propagation and geoeffectiveness at Earth, using the SWASTi framework. We perform a systematically sampled ensemble of 400 global magnetohydrodynamic simulations by varying the initial CME density, speed, magnetic flux and temperature. We quantify the relative influence of these parameters on CME evolution, plasma properties at L1, and the resulting geomagnetic response. The analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: initial speed primarily controls the peak radial velocity and arrival time at L1, magnetic flux controls the magnetic-field strength, and density governs the peak density and magnetopause compression. Primary parameters account for only half the output variance, highlighting the collective influence of other parameters. Density exhibits the broadest influence across the analyzed outputs. We find a mean arrival-time sensitivities of 2.43h per 100 km/s variation in injection speed and 1.99h per $10^{-18}$ kg/m$^3$ variation in injection density. The CME volume exhibits a two-phase evolution, characterized by an initial gradual expansion followed by a power-law regime with a median expansion index of 2.38. These results establish parameter-specific priorities for CME forecasting, highlighting the importance of constraining CME speed for arrival-time prediction, density for duration and pressure-driven effects, and magnetic flux for geomagnetic response at Earth.

papers.title: Cryogenic Optical Characteristics of S-FPL51 and S-LAH71: Refractive index, Transmission and Thermal expansion
papers.summary: Several near-infrared instruments on upcoming extremely large telescopes use a combination of OHARA S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass prisms to correct for the atmospheric differential refraction. Because large parts of these instruments are contained within a vessel cooled to liquid nitrogen temperatures, the changes in optical and mechanical properties should be considered during the design phase. In this report, we provide an update to our continuing efforts to characterize the S-FPL51 and S-LAH71 glass under cryogenic conditions. These efforts include a measurement of the refractive index (293 K, 100 K and 80 K), transmission measurements (293 K, 77 K and 43 K) and a determination of the coefficient of thermal expansion (between 293 K and 45 K). We will describe the cryogenic test setups that we have used to obtain our results, and provide summarizing equations of these material properties. This characterization will prove useful for conceptual design trade-offs, mechanical interface solutions and detailed optical design for future near-infrared instrumentation on large telescopes.

papers.title: As a matter of reconstruction -- varying the magnetic Prandtl number in implicit large eddy simulations
papers.summary: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} \not\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

papers.title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
papers.summary: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

papers.title: High-efficiency photonic GHZ measurements with linear optics
papers.summary: Probabilistic and destructive Bell-measurements, also known as fusions, constitute a fundamental primitive for photonic quantum technologies. These operations rely only on pairwise photonic interference, whereas the computational power of photonic quantum systems originates from many-body interference. Here, we introduce a family of high-efficiency linear-optical GHZ measurements based on four-mode interferometers and show that incorporating many-body interference into this ubiquitous primitive leads to more efficient entangling operations. For the four-photon case, the success probability is $9/32$, and adaptive variants ensure that unsuccessful events project onto useful stabilizer states. We further show that the approach naturally generalizes to larger GHZ measurements, yielding an exponentially higher success probability than previous linear-optical schemes. Finally, we demonstrate practical advantages for graph-state resource generation, entanglement distribution between remote spin-photon interfaces, and fusion-based quantum computing. Our results establish high-efficiency many-body measurements as a new primitive for scalable photonic quantum information processing.

papers.title: Hyperbolic embedding of higher-order simplicial networks
papers.summary: Many biological interactions involve groups rather than pairs, as when several proteins assemble into a multi-protein complex. Simplicial complexes naturally capture these collective interactions. Existing hyperbolic embeddings represent network hierarchy and similarity through a few interpretable coordinates, but rely only on pairwise links: they cannot distinguish three units engaged in a common interaction from three units connected only in pairs. We introduce here the hyperbolic higher-order (HHO) embedding, which embeds a simplicial complex into the Poincar\'e disk, while incorporating its group interactions. The hyperbolic area of the triangle spanned by three interacting nodes then measures how compactly their interaction is represented. Testson synthetic and real-world networks, including a co-authorship network and the protein interaction network of \textit{Escherichia coli}, show that HHO reduces the hyperbolic area of triangles representing simplices relative to those obtained from pairwise network embeddings. HHO also recovers node groups more accurately than pairwise embeddings and a weighted-clique alternative, with performance competitive with Euclidean embeddings, while providing a low-dimensional representation that can be analyzed with the tools of network geometry.

papers.title: Dipolar Exciton Polarons in a van der Waals Homobilayer
papers.summary: Fermi polarons exemplify how many-body interactions give rise to emergent quasiparticles, providing a fundamental framework for understanding interacting quantum matter. In electron-doped two-dimensional semiconductors, exciton polarons offer optical access to Fermi-polaron physics and electrical tunability, yet achieving stronger and more controllable exciton-electron interactions remains a key challenge. Here, we realize dipolar exciton polarons in an electrically tunable van der Waals homobilayer, where interlayer excitons with spatially separated electrons and holes act as quantum impurities carrying permanent electric dipole moments. These dipolar polarons exhibit substantially enhanced exciton-electron interactions, with binding energies more than four times those of conventional intralayer exciton polarons. We further demonstrate that Fermi-sea layer polarization provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling many-body interactions. In particular, the presence of a Fermi sea induces hybridization between oppositely oriented dipolar polarons, whereas confining the Fermi sea to a single layer suppresses this hybridization and produces orientation-selective many-body dressing. Our findings establish an experimental platform for dipolar-polaron physics in which dipole orientation and Fermi-sea layer polarization jointly govern many-body interactions, opening a route towards electrically tunable interactions and dipolar-polaron-mediated attraction between itinerant electrons.

papers.title: Inferring dominant acceleration mechanisms using the longitudinal spread of solar particle intensities: 28 May 2021 event
papers.summary: Solar energetic particles (SEPs) are typically accelerated during solar eruptions and propagate along magnetic field lines in the inner heliosphere. These eruptions include shock waves driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and magnetic reconnection in solar flares. Disentangling these source mechanisms within the measurements has been a long-standing problem for space physics researchers. Since spacecraft rarely reach the acceleration regions close to the Sun, measured SEP intensities reflect a combination of particle acceleration and interplanetary transport. The method used in this study attempts to identify which of the two main acceleration processes is more dominant for specific particle energies and species in a standalone event. Through this approach, we aim to better identify the signatures associated with these two acceleration phenomena and recognize similar behaviors in measurements with transport effects. This study characterizes the longitudinal spread of the SEP event on 28 May 2021 by fitting Gaussian curves at regular time intervals to particle intensities as a function of spacecraft position. This evolution offers unprecedented detail compared to earlier peak-focused studies, which were also limited to only three observers, while we now benefit from a novel fleet. To support the interpretation of the evolving profiles, we use a 2D SEP transport model to test if the evolution of the SEP distribution can also be caused by interplanetary effects. For this event, we find that the particle distribution of 0.1 MeV electrons remains static, while for 14 and 32 MeV protons, the distribution grows and moves to the west. We suggest that the CME-driven shock is the dominant source for protons, and that the flare is the dominant source only for the studied 0.1 MeV electrons. Interplanetary transport processes could also be contributing to the moving particle distributions.

papers.title: Decay of space plasma turbulence downstream of bow shocks: MMS magnetosheath unbiased campaign observations
papers.summary: Turbulence properties in the solar wind change with increasing heliospheric distance. Observations from different missions have shown how spectral indices converge towards a $f^{-5/3}$ spectrum in the inertial range as the solar wind reaches one astronomical unit, and how the cascade rate decays as the plasma moves away from the Sun. We evaluate whether these properties display similar trends in a smaller astrophysical system, that of a planetary magnetosheath. Using data from the 2023 Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) unbiased magnetosheath campaign, we determine the evolution of the spectral indices and the cascade rate along 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings. WIND observations permitted to monitor the state of the solar wind during the campaign and allowed to study the impact of the upstream plasma conditions on the evolution of the cascade rate downstream the bow shock. Our results show an increase of the cascade rate between two to three orders of magnitude after the plasma crosses the bow shock into the magnetosheath. Once in the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing distance to the bow shock in a way similar to solar wind observations, despite the smaller size of the system. Incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates of the cascade rate show a clear power-law decay of the cascade rate in the magnetosheath, particularly for the cases with upstream slow wind. This suggests that the way energy is injected into the system plays a role in the decay of turbulence as the plasma moves away from the bow shock.

papers.title: Creating functional nanostructures for vortex manipulation in superconducting Bi$_\text{2}$Sr$_\text{2}$CaCu$_\text{2}$O$_\text{8+x}$ thin films via focused He ion beam irradiation
papers.summary: Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+x}$ (Bi-2212) is a highly anisotropic high-temperature superconductor exhibiting unique vortex dynamics due to its layered structure. Precise nanoscale patterning of ultrathin Bi-2212 films remains challenging, limiting controlled studies of vortex pinning. Here, we employ 30 keV focused helium ion beam (He-FIB) irradiation to fabricate periodic arrays of columnar defects with 100 nm spacings in optimally-doped Bi-2212 thin films, thereby creating artificial vortex pinning centers. Magnetotransport measurements reveal pronounced vortex matching effects, evidenced by minima in magnetoresistance and peaks in critical current at commensurate magnetic fields. The angular dependence of magnetoresistance and critical current scale with an effective magnetic field, indicating strong confinement of pancake vortices along irradiation-induced tracks. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of He-FIB nanopatterning in modulating the superconducting properties in Bi-2212 thin films, providing a platform for fundamental studies of vortex matter and advancing prospects for device applications based on this highly anisotropic superconductor.

papers.title: Generative sampling with physics-informed kernels
papers.summary: We construct a generative network for Monte-Carlo sampling in lattice field theories and beyond, for which the layerwise propagation is computed and optimised independently on each layer. The architecture uses physics-informed renormalisation group flows that provide access to the layerwise propagation step from one layer to the next in terms of a simple first order partial differential equation for the respective renormalisation group kernel through a given layer. Thus, it transforms the generative task into that of solving once the set of independent and linear differential equations for the kernels of the transformation. As these equations are analytically known, the kernels can be refined iteratively. This allows us to structurally tackle out-of-domain problems generally encountered in generative models and opens the path to further optimisation. We illustrate the practical feasibility of the architecture within simulations in scalar field theories.

papers.title: Recommendation Feedback Loops Shape Urban Income Segregation and Venue Visitation
papers.summary: Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.

papers.title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths I: Energy Dissipation
papers.summary: In this work, we study the turbulent origin of ion-scale Current Sheets (CSs) and the dissipation of energy via magnetic reconnection. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ ion data from Solar Orbiter, collected between July 2020 and September 2022. We apply an automatic detection algorithm that finds current sheets (CSs) of thickness (length in the normal direction, $\lambda$) near the ion inertial length ($\delta_i$), and classifies them as Alfv\'enic or reconnecting. We compile a catalog of 974 CSs of thickness in the range of few to 90 ion inertial lengths, of which 53 contain an ion reconnection jet. We estimate that Solar Orbiter spends $\sim 1 \%$ of the dwell time inside a CS of few to 90 $\delta_i$ thickness, and 0.06\% inside a reconnecting CS of the same thickness range. By comparing these results with previous studies we estimate that the abundance of CSs and of Reconnecting CSs evolves with heliocentric distance ($r$) as $r^{-0.9}$ and $r^{-1.5}$, respectively. We estimate that magnetic reconnection dissipates $\epsilon_{rec}\sim 30 \hspace{5pt} \text{J} \text{kg}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1},$ in the $\sim 1 - 40$ $\delta_i$ scale-range, by assessing the amount of plasma that interacts with a reconnection exhaust. We show how the dissipation of turbulence energy cascade by magnetic reconnection at scales smaller than 90 $\delta_i$ is more effective closer to the Sun, and decays as $r^{-3.6}$. The current density of Alfv\'enic CSs thicker than the ion inertial length presents scale invariance, obeying $J_0/J_A=0.9(\lambda/2\delta_i)^{-0.71}$, suggesting that CSs generated locally from solar wind turbulence.

papers.title: Locality, Probability and the Relevance of History
papers.summary: Relativistic theory and experiments teach us that causal influences are constrained by the speed of light. Deterministic theories incorporate this lesson in $\textit{functional}$ terms: whether an event occurs or not is functionally determined by events that occur in its immediate causal past. In this paper we suggest a natural generalization of this constraint that applies to probabilistic theories: the $\textit{probability}$ that an event occurs is to be functionally determined by the $\textit{probability}$ of the event-occurrences in its immediate causal past. This constraint differs from Bell's criterion of local causality and turns out to imply it only under an additional assumption that requires history to be, in a sense, $\textit{ir}$relevant. Bell-inequality-violating quantum phenomena are thus arguably $\textit{not}$ in tension with relativity, locality, "statistical independence", nor with a supposed "realism". What they instead show is that history is, in a sense, $\textit{relevant}$.

papers.title: Microswimmers lose by swimming selfishly
papers.summary: At low Reynolds number, microswimmers are coupled by the flows they create, even when they are apart. The best way for each swimmer to push itself forward then depends on its neighbors, turning swimming together into a game. To study this, we optimize the shape changes of soft swimmers, alone and in pairs, with a differentiable Stokes solver. From random initial membrane motions, a lone swimmer converges to a traveling membrane wave. In a pair, the stroke of a swimmer affects its neighbor far more than the neighbor affects its own best stroke. For swimmers in line, this influence decays as $1/\ell$ with their separation $\ell$, whereas the incentive to respond decays as $1/\ell^2$. Selfish swimmers, which maximize their own payoff, respond only to the weak incentive. The cooperative gain they miss decays only as $1/\ell^2$, and their selfish adaptations leave the pair worse off than if both had kept their solitary strokes. Related swimmers, which also value the payoff of their neighbor, recover this gain, whereas competitors pay to hinder each other, both following a law that we derive analytically. Hydrodynamics alone thus makes swimming in company a social dilemma, whose outcome depends on how much the swimmers value each other.

papers.title: Drying kinematics selects open honeycomb fold networks on solvent-extracted viscoelastic thin films and gels
papers.summary: Solvent extraction and drying of substrate-supported viscoelastic films and gels produce quasiperiodic networks of three-armed surface folds. In this Letter, we examine the physical mechanisms governing their formation, length scales, and geometric organization. We observed that swelling-induced compression in the pinned film drives localized folding of a stiffening, diffusively thickening surface skin over a drained underlayer. Combining experiments and theory, we reveal that both the pattern wavelength and fold-arm length scale with the dried-film thickness following a power-law with an exponent 5/8, with remarkably weak dependence on elastic modulus. The folds form 120-degree junctions on a triangular lattice, defining an open honeycomb network whose pitch satisfies p = sqrt(3)(aL + g), where g is the junction gap. Notably, the folds accommodate less than 0.1% of the stored compressive strain, implicating elastocapillary arrest, rather than strain relaxation, in limiting their amplitude. These findings establish distinct geometric, kinetic, and interfacial constraints governing pattern selection in drying soft solids.

papers.title: The joint dynamics of Personal, Expressed and Social beliefs
papers.summary: Understanding belief dynamics is essential for dealing with societal phenomena from misperceptions and conflicts to polarization and stalemates in collective action. However, it is impeded by two main challenges. First, rich and largely qualitative knowledge about socio-cognitive processes involved in belief change and spread is insufficiently integrated into computational models of belief dynamics. Second, while numerous models of belief dynamics exist, they are rarely compared because of the differences in underlying theoretical frameworks and modeling choices. Here we address these two problems by developing a Personal, Expressed, and Social Beliefs (PES) meta-model in which personal beliefs co-evolve with one's expressed beliefs and perceived beliefs of others. It formalizes many critical socio-cognitive processes including authenticity, self-reinforcement, ego projection, social influence, conformity, validity, context effects, inertia, and potential and felt dissonance. It also enables principled comparison of a wide range of existing belief-dynamics models as its nested versions, from Voter, Ising, and DeGroot models, to bounded confidence and belief network models. We show how PES can be used to compare possible mechanisms underlying pluralistic ignorance, and find that it can occur when people conform their expressed beliefs to perceived beliefs of others, in particular when they have limited expressive repertoire (e.g., like, dislike, or stay silent). Counterintuitively, pluralistic ignorance can be dissolved when everyone ego-projects their own personal beliefs onto others to the same extent. Ego-projection generates misperception only when it is heterogeneous and covaries with personal beliefs. These results yield testable hypotheses and help predict when interventions will change personal, expressed, or social beliefs.

papers.title: Green building blocks reveal the complex anatomy of climate change mitigation technologies
papers.summary: Achieving net-zero emissions requires rapid innovation, yet the necessary technological knowhow is scattered across industries and countries. Comparing functionally similar green and nongreen patents, we identify "Green Building Blocks" (GBBs): modular components that can be added to reduce existing technologies' carbon footprints. These GBBs depict the anatomy of the green transition as a network that connects problems --- nongreen technologies --- to GBBs that mitigate their climate-change impact. Node degrees in this network are highly unequal, showing that the scope for climate-change mitigating innovation varies substantially across domains. The network helps predict which green technologies firms develop and maps which organizations hold complementary capabilities. The most complementary potential partners reside abroad for 84% of US firms, 87% of German firms, and 92% of Chinese firms, highlighting the importance of being able to collaborate across national borders.

papers.title: EnsAI: An Emulator for Atmospheric Ammonia Ensembles
papers.summary: Ensemble-based methods for data assimilation and emissions inversions are a popular way to encode flow-dependency within the model error covariance. While most ensemble methods do not require the use of an adjoint model, the need to repeatedly run a geophysical model to generate the ensemble can be a significant computational burden. In this paper, we introduce EnsAI, a new AI-based ensemble generation system for surface ammonia concentrations. When trained on an ensemble for ammonia generated by the GEM-MACH air quality model, it was shown that the ensembles produced by EnsAI can accurately reproduce the meteorology-dependent features of the original ensemble, while generating the ensemble 3,300 times faster than the original GEM-MACH ensemble. While EnsAI requires an upfront cost for generating the ensemble used for training, as well as the training itself, the long term computational savings can greatly exceed these initial computational costs. When used in an emissions inversion system, EnsAI produced similar inversion results to those in which the original GEM-MACH ensemble was used while using significantly less computational resources.

papers.title: What do the fundamental constants of physics tell us about life?
papers.summary: In the 1970s, the renowned physicist Victor Weisskopf famously developed a research program to qualitatively explain properties of matter in terms of the fundamental constants of physics. But there was one type of matter prominently missing from Weisskopf's analysis: life. Here, we develop Weisskopf-style arguments demonstrating how the fundamental constants of physics can be used to understand the properties of living systems. By combining biophysical arguments and dimensional analysis, we show that vital properties of chemical self-replicators, such as growth yield, minimum doubling time, and minimum power consumption in dormancy, can be quantitatively estimated using fundamental physical constants. The calculations highlight how the laws of physics constrain chemistry-based life on Earth, and if it exists, elsewhere in our universe.

papers.title: Minimal seed in supersonic boundary layer at $M=3$
papers.summary: This study investigates the minimal seed for laminar-to-turbulent transition in a supersonic boundary layer at $M=3.0$ and $Re=300$ using adjoint-based nonlinear non-modal analysis. While linear theory identifies oblique waves as the optimal disturbances for transient growth, we demonstrate that nonlinear effects fundamentally alter the optimal perturbation structure as the initial amplitude exceeds a critical threshold. Our analysis reveals that the nonlinear optimal perturbation exhibits a distinctive spatial distribution characterized by flattened structures in the outer layer and streamwise vortices near the wall, leading to a more rapid transition compared to the linear counterpart. A key finding is that this nonlinear amplification mechanism remains robust even under wall-cooled conditions ($T_w = 0.6 T_{ad}$), where the disappearance of the generalized inflection point (GIP) suppresses linear instabilities of Mack's first mode. This rapid growth is driven by the nonlinear interaction between two-dimensional planar waves near the wall and staggered vortex patterns in the outer layer, facilitating streak formation through vortex self-induction. Although the late-stage evolution eventually converges to the classical oblique breakdown scenario as characterized by the formation of $\Lambda$-vortices, the identified nonlinear path significantly reduces the disturbance energy required for transition.

papers.title: Effect of initial Rayleigh mode on drop deformation under impulsive acceleration
papers.summary: One of the fundamental ways of representing a droplet shape is through its Rayleigh-modes, where each mode corresponds to distinct surface-energy. Previous studies have focused on the effect of these modes on free oscillations of drops. In this paper, we systematically quantify how the different prescribed initial axisymmetric Rayleigh modes modulate aerodynamic energy uptake and the resulting deformation of an impulsively accelerated drop. Using experimentally validated VOF-based multiphase numerical simulations, we isolate the coupled effects of finite-amplitude surface oscillation modes and the associated initial surface-energy state by initialising the drops with well-defined $(n,0)$ modes and phases $\{0,\pi\}$, while conserving the equivalent drop volume. We find that the deformation outcome is governed by the drag due to the drop's initial geometry, and the dynamic coupling between the free modal oscillations and the forced aerodynamic deformation. We find that constructive superposition amplifies deformation, whereas destructive superposition can stabilise the drop even when the aerodynamic forcing is sufficient to deform an analogous spherical drop to breakup. Initial modes and phases that channel a larger fraction of the input power into deformation, in the form of oscillatory kinetic energy and additional surface energy, attain larger deformations and are closer to the fragmentation threshold. These couplings are especially pronounced in high-viscosity systems, where viscous dissipation is large and facilitates the transfer of a larger fraction of the total energy to translational kinetic energy instead of oscillatory kinetic energy. For low density-ratio systems, early-time coupling and energy transfer are the dominant mechanisms that govern drop deformation.
