papers.title: Wavelet Packet-Based Diffusion Model for Ground Motion Generation with Multi-Conditional Energy and Spectral Matching
papers.summary: Temporal energy distribution strongly affects nonlinear structural response and cumulative damage. We propose a multi-conditional diffusion framework for ground motion synthesis that simultaneously matches temporal energy evolution and target response spectra. Wavelet packet decomposition provides the signal representation and enables direct waveform reconstruction via orthogonal filter banks. A Transformer-based conditional encoder with cross-attention integrates heterogeneous conditions, including spectral ordinates, Arias intensity, temporal parameters, and Husid curves. The framework adopts the Elucidating Diffusion Model (EDM) with second-order Heun sampling to improve inference efficiency without sacrificing quality. Tests on the NGA-West2 database show that explicit temporal-energy constraints markedly improve control of energy onset and significant duration while preserving spectrum matching and maintaining stable diversity sampling. The framework yields spectrum-compatible motions with realistic energy evolution and supports uncertainty quantification via conditional diversity sampling.

papers.title: Deflation Techniques for Stellarator Equilibrium and Optimization
papers.summary: Stellarator optimization is a multi-objective, non-convex problem characterized by a complex objective landscape containing many local minima. The solution resulting from a single optimization is highly sensitive to factors such as the initial guess, objective weights, and the optimization method employed. However, merely varying these factors does not guarantee that a physically distinct minimum will be found; optimizations often fail to converge to good minima or simply return to the same or very similar local minima despite large-scale parameter scans. This paper presents a novel application of deflation methods to effectively explore this landscape. By modifying the objective function to penalize and "deflate" away already-found solutions, this technique encourages the optimizer towards attractive, distinct new minima while using a single initial guess and optimization setup. We provide a primer on deflation for nonlinear systems and non-convex optimization before applying it to non-axisymmetric equilibrium and stellarator optimization problems. Key results include the discovery of families of global equilibria with similar core characteristics and the convergence to helical core equilibria without prescient initial guesses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that augmenting stage-one stellarator and stage-two coil optimization with deflation constraints readily produces multiple high-quality, distinct solutions, establishing the method's efficacy and ease of use.

papers.title: Enhancing FRET through DNA-controlled Emitters and ENZ Metamaterials
papers.summary: Simultaneous nanoscale spatial control and macroscopic electromagnetic enhancement are critical for maximizing resonance energy transfer. However, conventional systems with photonic platforms suffer from stochastic emitter distributions and steep field gradients. Here we demonstrate a unified architecture combining programmable DNA molecular beacons with an epsilon near zero (ENZ) multilayer metamaterial. Using DNA scaffolds, donor-acceptor pairs (Atto425/Cy3.5) are structurally locked into closed (2 nm) and extended (8.16 nm) conformations within the ENZ near field. Time-resolved photoluminescence reveals accelerated donor decay and an increase in extended state FRET efficiency from 56.7% on glass to 79.4% on ENZ, corresponding to a 5.8 fold transfer rate acceleration. Electromagnetic Green tensor modeling confirms that ENZ boundary conditions strongly amplify dipole coupling within first few nm of the interface exhibiting pronounced orientation selectivity. This hybrid platform provides a deterministic orientational and spatial control for sculpting molecular-scale light-matter interactions.

papers.title: An abundance of periodic orbits in two-dimensional turbulence revealed by a diffusion-based generative model
papers.summary: Unstable periodic orbits offer a route to reconstructing the statistical properties of chaotic systems, including turbulence. Short periodic orbits are particularly important in periodic-orbit expansions, yet their abundance and diversity remain largely unexplored even in the extensively studied two-dimensional Kolmogorov flow. We search for short relative periodic orbits in this flow at $Re=40$, considering all distinct classes of recurrence symmetry. We train a generative diffusion model on nonperiodic vorticity sequences from a direct numerical simulation of turbulence, producing time series that resemble physically plausible trajectories. The model incorporates symmetry properties of the system but is otherwise trained solely on these data, without enforcing the governing equations. After training, we modify its architecture to generate synthetic trajectories that are periodic up to spatial symmetry transformations, without retraining its weights. These synthetic trajectories are then refined into exact solutions using an iterative solver, yielding 111 new relative periodic orbits with periods $T < 3$, including 40 with $T<2$. Rather than revealing a hierarchy dominated by a small number of short cycles, this abundance suggests that quantitatively converged periodic-orbit descriptions of spatiotemporal chaos may require substantially larger orbit libraries than anticipated.

papers.title: Accurate Vector Magnetometer via Zeeman Rabi Oscillations
papers.summary: Accurate magnetic field direction sensing in compact platforms is critical in applications spanning magnetic navigation, space science, and biomedical imaging. We demonstrate a single-optical-axis vector optically pumped magnetometer based on Rabi oscillations between Zeeman sublevels driven by a series of resonant radiofrequency (RF) polarization ellipses (PEs). A calibration protocol based on controlled rotations of the DC magnetic field determines the spatial orientation of each PE. We develop a detailed theoretical model describing the angular dependence of the Rabi frequencies, incorporating key systematics including RF Stark shifts and Bloch-Siegert shifts. We also account for an RF-based heading-error systematic affecting Rabi-frequency measurements arising from the nonlinear Zeeman effect. Simultaneous Larmor measurements yield the magnitude of the magnetic field, enabling integrated vector-scalar measurements. The magnetometer achieves deadzone-free vector operation with 80 $\mu$rad mean angular accuracy and angular noise densities as low as 8 $\mu$rad$/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, offering a pathway towards miniaturized sensors without requiring 3D optical access or sensor rotations.

papers.title: Engineering the Frozen Mode Near a Stationary Inflection Point in Coupled Single-Mode Waveguides with Lateral Gratings
papers.summary: We introduce a systematic approach to designing slow-light photonic integrated circuits supporting a frozen mode associated with a third-order exceptional point of degeneracy (EPD), known as a stationary inflection point (SIP). The proposed approach employs three-way coupled waveguides incorporating lateral gratings and operating at telecommunication wavelengths. We investigate two distinct waveguide configurations and demonstrate the formation of SIPs through full-wave eigenmode simulations. We also analyze the sensitivity of the dispersion characteristics to geometric perturbations and realistic fabrication constraints. A periodic waveguide with integrated tapered terminations is fabricated and experimentally characterized, revealing spectral features that are qualitatively consistent with numerical predictions. Simulations of finite-length structures further demonstrate substantial group-delay enhancement near the SIP frequency. These results establish a practical approach to realizing frozen-mode waveguides and integrating SIP-based slow-light functionalities into silicon photonic circuits.

papers.title: FermiLink: An Agent Harness for Multidomain Scientific Simulations
papers.summary: Artificial-intelligence (AI) agent harnesses have been developed for autonomous scientific simulations, but most current agent harnesses are tested on single or a small set of software packages. Herein, FermiLink, an extensible open-source agent harness is introduced for multidomain scientific simulations. Its key design principle is the separation of package knowledge bases from simulation workflows, so that simulation workflows in FermiLink, from figure-level simulations to full-paper-level research on high-performance computing clusters, operate uniformly among supported packages via a four-layer progressive disclosure mechanism. This agent harness is specifically optimized for high performance computing (HPC) clusters, enabling multi-day multi-step scientific simulations in the absence of human intervention. Using OpenAI Codex as the agent provider, the capabilities of FermiLink are demonstrated across approximately 50 scientific software packages spanning nine research domains from chemistry to engineering. Systematic benchmarks on 132 real-world figure-level reproduction tasks with 44 packages show that FermiLink reproduces 74 (56.1%) of published figures with simulations, among which 30 (22.7%) achieve high-fidelity agreement and 35 reach qualitative agreement with the target figures. A smaller set of human expert-guided reproduction benchmarks with 10 packages in physics and chemistry further highlights the importance of expert insights for improving the simulation fidelity. Beyond reproduction, a single-blinded study demonstrates that FermiLink can produce research-grade results on unpublished polariton physics problems when provided with sufficiently detailed research objectives. Overall, FermiLink provides a scalable research infrastructure that may accelerate the path from scientific questions to computational results across diverse domains.

papers.title: On the curlometer measurement of field-aligned and perpendicular currents in low Earth orbit: Swarm observations and whole geospace simulations
papers.summary: Measuring field-aligned currents (FACs) using magnetic field observations provides a powerful means to probe the multi-scale interactions between the magnetosphere, ionosphere and thermosphere. In this study, we benchmark the curlometer technique using Swarm spacecraft observations and simulations of the coupled magnetosphere-ionosphere system. We begin by correlating current density curlometer estimates derived from Swarm tetrahedra with varying spatial scales and barycentre locations. This confirms an apparent departure from stationarity for FACs at spatio-temporal scales below 100 km where measurements appear highly uncorrelated. We then analyse simulated magnetic perturbations, where four-point measurements can always be constructed. This shows how, even at meso-scales of hundreds of kilometres, time-shifted FAC estimates can diverge significantly from this ground truth. In both observational and simulated data we find poor tetrahedral configurations can produce spurious perpendicular currents due to numerical instability in the inversion process. This can be mitigated using appropriate quality metrics and high-quality FAC reconstructions still achieved with a tetrahedral face well-aligned to the local magnetic field. These results highlight the dynamic nature of FACs at large as well as small scales, and underscore the substantial advantages of true four-point observations for their accurate analysis.

papers.title: CHIMERA: Couette Hydrodynamics for the Investigation of Multi-fluid Extreme-Reynolds Turbulence in Annuli
papers.summary: The CHIMERA (Couette Hydrodynamics for the Investigation of Multi-fluid Extreme-Reynolds Turbulence in Annuli) apparatus has been developed to investigate turbulent momentum transport in a canonical wall-driven flow using a wide variety of working fluids, from room-temperature gases to normal and superfluid helium. We present the design and characterization of a cryogenic Taylor-Couette facility in which torque is measured on a suspended outer cylinder using a torsion-pendulum sensor and a non-contact optical readout. This configuration avoids the need for cryogenic torque transducers or electrical instrumentation inside the cryostat while providing high sensitivity over a wide dynamic range. Measurements performed in gaseous helium at room temperature and in normal liquid helium reach Reynolds numbers up to 106 and agree well with established torque correlations, validating the apparatus over more than five decades in Reynolds number. Beyond providing such an exceptionally broad operating range with a single experimental facility and a single torque sensor, the principal motivation of CHIMERA is to enable direct comparisons of turbulent momentum transport in He I and He II under identical boundary conditions. By combining the same geometry and the same global torque diagnostic in both classical and quantum fluids, the apparatus provides a unique platform for investigating how wall-driven turbulence and its scaling evolve across the superfluid transition.

papers.title: Photon Calibration Techniques for High Resolution Cryogenic Detectors
papers.summary: Monoenergetic photons from a pulsed laser diode or LED are commonly used to calibrate the detector response of high-resolution calorimetric detectors. However, when the detector's resolution is larger than the energy of a single photon, a calibration is normally derived using Poisson statistics. In this paper, we clarify the assumptions implicit in this calibration method, before considering how a more realistic model of a detector's performance will violate these assumptions, biasing the calibration. Finally, we judge the individual impact of specific detector parameters on our calibration, and conclude with discussion of both the limits of our calculations and the implications for state-of-the art detectors.

papers.title: Quaternion Dirac--Coulomb--Breit Integral Transformation for Relativistic Four-Component Correlated Electronic Structure Theory
papers.summary: High-accuracy correlated four-component relativistic electronic structure methods are typically formulated in terms of integrals over molecular orbital (MO). Consequently, an efficient and scalable strategy is required to deal with the complexity of transforming relativistic two-electron integrals from the atomic orbital (AO) to the MO basis. The transformation bottleneck is particularly acute for approaches that include Breit interaction integrals, whose computational and memory demands further exacerbate the transformation cost. To overcome this challenge, we develop a quaternion-based, AO-driven direct integral transformation scheme. The method operates on scalar AO integrals and combines quaternion density-based contractions with direct Cauchy-Schwarz screening to systematically exploit integral locality. As a result, the proposed framework substantially lowers the practical computational scaling and provides an efficient, memory-conscious, and highly parallelizable pathway for the routine inclusion of relativistic Dirac-Coulomb-Breit integrals in large-scale four-component correlated calculations.

papers.title: Absolute intensity measurement of pulsed muon beams using in-beam activation
papers.summary: The absolute number of negative muons contained in a beam is essential for many experiments at accelerator facilities, but determining this number in pulsed beams has been difficult, particularly at high intensities. A method utilizing the yield of the $\beta$ delayed $\gamma$ rays from the residual nuclei following the muon nuclear capture reaction has recently been demonstrated for determining the muon number in the pulsed muon beam. In particular, the in-beam activation method employs isotopes with short lifetimes, enabling the beam intensity to be monitored during beam irradiation. However, the applicability of this method was limited because the required production branching ratio (BR) data were available only for a limited number of isotopes, restricting its use to specific experimental conditions. To broaden the applicability of this method, we searched for new candidate isotopes that are suitable for beam intensity measurement using the in-beam activation method and assessed their feasibility to a wide range of experiments. Based on the strength of the production BR, the muon capture probability, the practical detection efficiency of the detector, and the rarity of the target material in the surrounding structures, the reactions $^\mathrm{nat}$Ag ($\mu^-, \nu_\mu x$) $^{107m}$Pd and $^\mathrm{nat}$Pd ($\mu^-, \nu_\mu x$) $^{107m, 105m}$Rh are identified as a useful references for determining the number of muons in pulsed beams using the in-beam activation method.

papers.title: Flow-polarity decoupling and universal mobility enhancement in dense bacterial active fluids
papers.summary: Active fluids consisting of living cells or synthetic microswimmers display rich emergent behavior and nonequilibrium mechanical properties, which not only shed light on various biological processes but also inform the engineering of autonomous fluidics and self-driven materials. The individual behavior of microswimmers and their interaction with self-generated mesoscale solvent flows underlie the emergent properties of active fluids. Here we studied the microscopic dynamics in dense 3D bacterial active fluids by simultaneous imaging of cell body, flagella, and flow field. A surprising finding is that the polarity of cells was randomly distributed in mesoscale flow regimes, and yet the system displays mesoscale order in the self-generated solvent flows. Despite the apparent flow-polarity decoupling, the motion of cells relative to local solvent flows predominantly navigated upstream, with the self-advection speed overall enhanced by a flow-controlled constant. Numerical modeling with full hydrodynamic interactions reveals that the observed flow-polarity decoupling arises from the breakdown of the commonly held force-dipole assumption for anisotropic microswimmers: in the presence of flow gradient and near-field hydrodynamic interactions, the direction of total active forcing exerted by a swimming bacterium to the surrounding fluid no longer aligns with its polarity. The simulations suggest that near-field interactions serve as a new type of emergent, configuration-dependent active forcing, which profoundly impact self-organization and transport in dense bacterial suspensions. Taken together, our work establishes fundamental knowledge for faithfully understanding the collective behavior of dense polar active fluids.

papers.title: Scenario-conditioned flow matching for probabilistic generation of three-component ground-motion waveforms
papers.summary: Performance-based seismic risk assessment requires three-component acceleration histories compatible with specified source, path, and site conditions. Conventional ground-motion prediction equations provide scalar intensity measures, while many generative waveform models learn amplitude and waveform shape within a single high-dimensional target. We present WaveFlowGMM, a two-stage probabilistic ground-motion model that uses peak ground acceleration (PGA) as an amplitude interface between scenario conditioning and waveform generation. The amplitude stage uses physics-informed symbolic learning to estimate component-wise PGA medians and a full cross-component covariance. The waveform stage uses few-step AlphaFlow in an invertible wavelet-packet coefficient space to generate normalised three-component histories that are rescaled by sampled PGA. Tests on an event-level NGA-West2 holdout set show that the generated motions recover the main magnitude, distance, and site scaling, keep peak and spectral residuals close to zero, preserve three-component amplitude dependence, and yield velocity and displacement histories without systematic drift after integration of the generated three-component acceleration histories. The framework provides an interpretable and computationally efficient candidate component for waveform-level seismic hazard and risk analysis.

papers.title: Motion-Based Self-Normalisation Enables Precision Nanoparticle Sizing
papers.summary: Label-free all-optical nanosizing based on interferometric or darkfield-imaging infers particle size, composition, or shape from single-particle scattering signals. These signals are, however, scaled by a spatially varying normalisation profile that combines the non-uniform illumination with position-dependent detection and data-processing effects. Common normalisation strategies estimate this profile from a direct measurement of the illumination field or background. This is not possible in background-free geometries, such as side- or light-sheet-type illumination, where the illumination does not reach the detector. Here we introduce a self-normalisation method that reconstructs the normalisation profile from the scattering signals of freely diffusing nanoparticles, without additional hardware or calibration samples. To remove the bias caused by particle-to-particle heterogeneity, single-particle trajectories are normalised against each other in regions of spatial overlap, where distinct particles sample the same normalisation profile. In a transmission geometry, the reconstructed profile agrees qualitatively with a direct illumination measurement and reduces signal variations within single trajectories from 6.5% to 2.0% (one sigma), corresponding to a diameter uncertainty of about 0.7%. Under 90-degree side-illumination, where the illumination field cannot be measured through the detection path, normalisation with the reconstructed 3D profile reduces within-trajectory signal variations from about 30% to 4-10% across most of the sampled volume. As the method solely relies on the scattering signal already acquired, our approach is directly compatible with existing interferometric and darkfield nanoscopy platforms and extendable to other scattering or fluorescent modalities, including light-sheet microscopy.

papers.title: Putting PASPT2 on a Firmer Basis
papers.summary: The recently proposed partial-active-space (PAS) multi-state second-order perturbation theory (PASPT2) [Precis. Chem. 4, 997 (2026)] features connected amplitudes and a connected, closed intermediate Hamiltonian. Despite these hallmarks, PASPT2 (denoted as PASPT2H from now on) is not strictly size-extensive, as originally thought (and numerically confirmed), albeit strictly size-consistent. Nevertheless, PASPT2 is near-extensive for the states with major projections on the chosen PAS $\mathcal{M}_0$. This becomes more transparent upon introducing PASPT2X, a strictly size-extensive variant. Compared with the intruder-prone PASPT2X, the intruder-free PASPT2H merely neglects the second-order corrections that are important only for those states with major projections on the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{R}_X$ of $\mathcal{M}_0$ within the closed space $\mathcal{M}_X$ ($=\mathcal{M}_0\oplus\mathcal{R}_X$); however, such states are not supported by the chosen finite one-particle basis set. The weak violation of size-extensivity is therefore numerically insignificant for the target states supported by $\mathcal{M}_0$, reinforcing the theoretical basis of PASPT2H.

papers.title: Chiral vibrational modes and vibrational circular dichroism
papers.summary: The recent interest in chiral phonons in a variety of physical phenomena and their hypothesized role in the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect [Phys. Rev. Research, 5, L022039 (2023)] call for further investigation into the chirality of molecular vibrations. Although molecular chirality has conventionally been quantified using structural properties, recent work has highlighted the role of dynamical response properties as chirality metrics. In this work, we examine an inter-atom helicity pseudoscalar as a complementary measure of vibrational chirality, associated with the vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) intensity in the fixed partial charge (FPC) approximation. This pseudoscalar is translationally and rotationally invariant, can distinguish between opposite enantiomers, and unlike an atomic pseudoscalar measure considered in our earlier work [Phys. Rev. Lett., 133, 268001 (2024)] does not rely on a predefined symmetry axis. For a twisted ethane model as well as several small molecules, this pseudoscalar correlates well with structural descriptors based on the continuous chirality measure. Overall, our results support response-based metrics as a physically meaningful and practically useful characterization of vibrational chirality. Importantly, while the FPC-based VCD estimate provides a useful quantifier of vibrational chirality, we show that it is a rather poor predictor of the actual molecular VCD response because the latter is strongly influenced by the (vibrational configuration-dependent) molecular electronic response.

papers.title: Performance of an HRPPD in Tesla-scale magnetic fields
papers.summary: High-Rate Picosecond Photodetectors (HRPPDs) are state-of-the-art microchannel-plate (MCP) photodetectors that offer excellent timing and spatial resolution, together with high single-photon detection efficiency. They are currently being considered for the ePIC experiment at the future Electron Ion Collider (EIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory. A key requirement for the application of this technology is reliable operation in a strong magnetic field up to 1.5 T, with magnetic flux lines at an inclination of $\le15^\circ$ to the normal of the MCP surface. Magnetic field-induced distortions of the collected charge in MCP-based detectors can be compensated by tuning the operating parameters; however, the objective of this study is to quantify this performance in the case of the EIC-HRPPD, a particular MCP stack-up specialized for operation within ePIC. This photosensor employs a high quantum efficiency photocathode, 10$~\mu$m capillary pores, narrow transfer gaps, and a custom ceramic pixelated DC-coupled readout. This article explores the optimal operating parameters (mainly the voltages applied across the gaps and the MCPs) for single photon detection at various inclination angles in a uniform field up to 1.8 T. Ultimately, it was found that the gain and single photon detection efficiency of the HRPPD could be recovered over a range of polar inclination angles up to $\pm35^\circ$.

papers.title: Momentum-scalar coupled turbulence with anomalous momentum and scalar diffusions. Part 2: With short-range external force and implementation in electrokinetic turbulence
papers.summary: We extend the generalized anomalous diffusion framework established in Part 1 to the short-range forcing regime ($\beta>2/3$), where the multiscale-force dominated (MFD) subrange is intercalated after the inertial subrange, competing directly with the dissipation ranges. Focusing on electrokinetic (EK) turbulence as the prototypical example with $\beta=1$, we derive the relations for the velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers, $k_{\mathrm{MD}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{SD}}$, across all four subranges of the Quad-cascade process (inertial, constant-$\Pi_u$, constant-$\Pi_s$, and variable flux). By incorporating Golestanian's predicted anomalous diffusion regimes for electrolytes, we construct comprehensive phase diagrams showing how the relative magnitudes of $k_{\mathrm{MD}}$ and $k_{\mathrm{SD}}$ are governed by the scale-dependent anomalous Schmidt number $\mathrm{Sc}_Z$. We identify two new spectral subranges that emerge exclusively in this short-range forcing regime: (i) the convective-forcing-viscous subrange ($k_{\mathrm{MU}}\ll k\ll k_{\mathrm{CFVD}}$) for either $\mathrm{Sc}_Z\gg1$ or $\mathrm{Sc}_Z\ll1$ with $\gamma>\alpha$, where the scalar field drives viscous flow through electric body force; and (ii) the diffusive-forcing-convective subrange ($k_{\mathrm{MU}}\ll k\ll k_{\mathrm{DFCD}}$) for $\mathrm{Sc}_Z\ll1$ and $\gamma\le\alpha$, where the scalar structure dominated by diffusion determines electric body force, which in turn causes momentum convection. These results provide a complete analytical map of EK turbulence under anomalous diffusion, revealing how external parameters such as electric field strength and ionic diffusivity determine the cascade topology.

papers.title: Solar Magnetic Configuration Control over Radiation Belt Electrons
papers.summary: Earth is surrounded by two highly dynamic concentric belts of particle radiation. The outer radiation belt exhibits coherent variability at solar-cycle, seasonal, and 27-day (Carrington) timescales. While the solar-cycle and Carrington variations have been attributed to the recurrence of coronal hole solar wind, the seasonal variation has long been explained by local geometric effects that modulate the solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. Here, we challenge this paradigm by showing that the periodic recurrence of coronal hole solar wind likewise drives the seasonal variation. We further demonstrate that the Alfv\'enic nature of this solar wind is a key driver of the observed electron flux enhancement in the outer radiation belt. These findings provide a unifying framework linking solar magnetic topology, solar wind properties, and magnetospheric dynamics across multiple timescales at Earth and beyond.

papers.title: Iterative Construction of n-Dimensional Navier-Stokes Solutions with Non-Gradient Convection
papers.summary: Exact periodic solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations arise when the convective field is a pure gradient and can be absorbed into the pressure. We construct solutions outside this class, in arbitrary spatial dimension, by an iteration in which each step solves a linear diffusion problem forced by the transverse part of the preceding convective field. The construction is dimension-independent, and for a cyclic family of initial fields the first two iterates are available in closed form. Carried out numerically in three dimensions, the iteration converges: at Re = 10 successive iterates contract with an observed factor 0.43 and the limit is a fixed point of the discretised map to a relative defect of 8.2 x 10^-5. The observed factor exceeds unity by Re = 30, which identifies the practical range of the iteration rather than a proved convergence boundary. We also show what goes wrong when the projection is omitted, as it was in an earlier iteration of the author's: the iterates cease to be divergence-free and an apparent growth appears that belongs to the expansion and not to the flow. For an n-dimensional generalisation of the initial field the fraction of the convective field not absorbed by pressure is exactly 2*sqrt(2)/3 in every dimension n >= 3, and the longitudinal fraction exactly 1/3. The divergence of each returned source is a sharp diagnostic, failing by sixteen orders of magnitude at the step where the projection is omitted; the cell kinetic energy is a weaker one, detecting gross failure only.

papers.title: Is Your AI Fast Enough to Run a Fusion Reactor?
papers.summary: In magnetic confinement fusion, compact machine learning algorithms are often integrated into the control loop on CPU-based custom hardware stacks. Deterministic implementations of these algorithms target instabilities which can evolve over microseconds to milliseconds. Staying within this framework may therefore limit the pace of control-system development to the inference time available. With the expansion of hardware acceleration and large models, we aim to bring ML models for fusion control to modern inference engines and compare, based on the physics reactor, the suitability of each engine per model. This study implements a consistent real-time machine learning algorithm for GPUs and optimized CPU packages, including OpenVINO, XLA, and TVM, at DIII-D National Fusion Facility. For the smallest model, one CPU core responds within 3.6 $\mu$s in 99% of control cycles and an NVIDIA A100 within 28 $\mu$s. We also evaluate models running simultaneously, as they would run in a typical experiment, and find best use cases per framework.

papers.title: Learning the information contained in the microstructure of data distributions
papers.summary: Understanding how much and where information is nested in sets of data obtained using different parameters and metrics is a typical problem in the analysis of high-dimensional datasets. Approaches based on relative data-driven metrics may be poorly quantitative and difficult to interpret, while accurate methods may be computationally expensive and impractical for large datasets. Here, we report an efficient, quantitative, and transferable method useful to this end, which we call "Micro-Information Analysis". Its foundation is based on the tight relationship that exists between the microscopic features of data distributions and the information they contain. The method performs preliminary unsupervised clustering, capturing microstructural features of data distributions such as the dominant Gaussian microdomains (microstates) present in them, their population, separation, and their residual non-Gaussian fraction. Leveraging the principle of clustering-and-minimization of Shannon entropy, this allows quantifying in bit (that is, in absolute metric) the information contained in the microstructure of the data, and how much information is nested in each Gaussian and non-Gaussian microdomain. The output of the analysis is a set of easily interpretable Information-Microstructure plots that allow to readily compare and rank data based on their information content and to graphically map the information breakdown among their various microenvironments in diagrams that are easy to interpret. We prove the efficiency of our method by analyzing and ranking data generated synthetically or from molecular simulations, demonstrating how "Micro-Information Analysis" is a physically-grounded quantitative tool useful for the study of physical systems from their data and for data science in general.

papers.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
papers.summary: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. The root of the problem is nonlocality of filtering, which compares directions in different tangent planes. The same reason underlies the Foucault pendulum's precession, and it is why the commutation failure is intrinsically geometric rather than being due to the coordinate system or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

papers.title: Stochastic Analysis of Laser Phase Noise in Photonics-Assisted Radio Frequency Beamforming
papers.summary: This paper develops a stochastic model for quantifying the impact of laser phase noise on photonics-assisted radio frequency (RF) beamforming. Unlike conventional deterministic models, the presented theoretical framework captures the statistical randomness associated with the RF array factor of beamforming networks driven by finite-linewidth lasers. Fourier-domain analysis reveals that laser phase noise reshapes the spatial coherence function of such beamforming networks, inducing coherent RF aperture shrinkage, beam-pattern distortion, and directivity degradation. The analysis highlights that beamforming network architectures employing nanosecond-scale optical differential delays can exhibit substantial performance degradation even when driven by commercially available narrow-linewidth (kHz-range) lasers. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that average RF power gain gets downscaled and fluctuations dominate in large-aperture beamforming networks due to phase noise, imposing an upper limit on the maximum achievable RF antenna array-size. The reported results highlight the quantitative performance and scalability limits imposed by laser phase noise in photonics-assisted RF beamforming, offering key design guidelines for implementing large-scale beamforming networks in next-generation wireless communications, sensing, radar, and radio astronomy applications.

papers.title: Mode-2 solitary waves in continuous stratifications
papers.summary: Computed herein are examples of mode-2 internal solitary waves to the Dubreil-Jacotin-Long (DJL) equation. These are localised, fully nonlinear waves in a continuously stratified, inviscid fluid under the Boussinesq and rigid-lid approximations. The equation is solved directly using finite differences on a periodic domain, enabling the computation of both generalised solitary waves, which possess oscillatory mode-1 tails, and embedded solitary waves, whose tails vanish. Two stratifications are considered. The first is a double pycnocline, generalising the three-layer system considered by Doak et al. (2022) by replacing each infinitesimal interface with a pycnocline of finite thickness. The second stratification, a surface mixed layer above an exponentially stratified layer, shows that embedded mode-2 solitary waves are not restricted to double-pycnocline stratifications. These are the first mode-2 solitary waves of the DJL equation computed for stratifications that are asymmetric about mid-depth.

papers.title: El Agente Quntur: Agentic Active-Space Selection for CASSCF
papers.summary: Multireference calculations require time-consuming expert decisions about active spaces, state identity, and convergence. This study asks whether agents can make these decisions reliably. Using the El Agente Quntur multi-agent harness with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra as its language models, agents study 32 fixed-geometry singlet excitations, detect missing active orbitals, compare excited states, and revise state assignments as calculations progress. Prompts specify equal-weight two-singlet state-averaged complete active space self-consistent field (CASSCF) calculations followed by strongly contracted second-order N-electron valence state perturbation theory (NEVPT2) with def2-TZVPD; agents choose and refine the active spaces. Excitation energies are evaluated against published complete active space second-order perturbation theory (CASPT2) reference values at matching geometries. Agentic execution reduces mean absolute error by 48\% relative to six deterministic Active Space Finder protocols. Computational traces vary substantially across runs in selection strategies and cost, even for the same molecule. These results underscore the advantage of agentic active space selection over fixed workflows, yet leave room to improve efficiency through runtime-aware decision-making, reduced inter-agent communication overhead and redundancy, more systematic checks of state identity, and clearer stopping criteria.

papers.title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
papers.summary: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.

papers.title: Searching for Ultra-Light Axions with Twisted Cavity Resonators of Anyon Rotational Symmetry with Bulk Modes of Non-Zero Helicity
papers.summary: M\"obius-ring resonators stem from a well-studied geometrical structure with a one-sided topology, the M\"obius strip, and have been shown to exhibit fermion rotational symmetry with respect to an untwisted ring resonator, which exhibits boson rotational symmetry [1]. Here, we present twisted hollow resonators with equilateral triangular cross-sections, leading to cavities with anyon rotational symmetry. Unlike conventional cavity resonators, these structures permit bulk resonant modes with a non-zero complex electromagnetic overlap $\mathcal C_p=\int_V\mathbf{E}_p\cdot\mathbf{B}_p^*\,d\tau$. The real and imaginary parts of this overlap couple to different observable quadratures. Although the negative-frequency component of a real axion field is immaterial for haloscopes employing a static DC magnetic field, it must be retained for a pumped resonator because the complex forms of Maxwell's equations differ for positive and negative frequencies and produce distinct upper and lower mixing branches. Retaining both branches shows that the real overlap produces amplitude-modulated sidebands, whereas the imaginary helicity of the modes studied here produces phase-modulated sidebands through the axion-photon chiral anomaly. A sensitive ultra-light dark-matter experiment may therefore be realised with an ultra-stable oscillator and a phase-sensitive readout. The sensitivity curves calculated here require the assumed noise floor to be interpreted as phase-modulation noise rather than amplitude-modulation noise, and consequently require sufficiently low residual oscillator phase noise at the axion Fourier frequency. The scheme removes the usual requirement for an external magnetic field and permits superconducting resonators with reduced surface loss and enhanced axion sensitivity.

papers.title: Resonant analogue configurations in atomic condensates
papers.summary: As a contribution to a memorial volume, we provide a comprehensive discussion of resonant configurations in analogue gravity, focusing on its implementation in atomic condensates and combining review features with original insights and calculations. In particular, we jointly analyze the analogues of the Andreev and Hawking effects using a microscopic description based on the Bogoliubov approximation. We perform a detailed study of the thermality of the Andreev and Hawking spectra for canonical black-hole solutions, finding that both can be described by a gray-body distribution to a very good approximation. We contemplate several resonant scenarios whose efficiency to enhance anomalous scattering processes is compared to that of non-resonant setups. The presence of quantum signatures in analogue configurations, such as the violation of Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities or entanglement, is analyzed, observing that resonant configurations highly increase the entanglement signal, especially for the Andreev effect. We also discuss how these results have served as inspiration for the rapidly expanding field of quantum information in high-energy colliders. Finally, we study the physics of black-hole lasers as further examples of resonant analogue structures, distinguishing three stages in its time evolution. For short times, we compute the linear and non-linear spectrum for different models. For intermediate times, we generalize the current analysis of the BHL-BCL crossover. For long times, we discuss the emerging concept of spontaneous Floquet state and its potential implications.

papers.title: Counting statistics and inference limits for reactions driven by latent ergodic dynamics
papers.summary: Many natural phenomena--from chemical reactions to biological encounters and sensor detections--are described through counts of discrete events. Such events occur at random times when an underlying, often unobserved, dynamical system enters a reactive region of its phase space. Despite the ubiquity of these processes in nature, a general framework linking counting statistics to the properties of the underlying stochastic process is lacking. Most existing theories, including widely used mass-action models, neglect trajectory correlations and assume independent counts. We develop a theory that overcomes these limitations, deriving a general expression for the inter-count time distribution as a function of the spatiotemporal scales of the reactive region and the stochastic process. The counting statistics interpolate between a reaction-limited regime, where counts are effectively independent and follow Poisson statistics, and a diffusion-limited regime, where counts are strongly determined by the correlation structure of the latent stochastic process and exhibit systematic overdispersion relative to the Poissonian limit. This structure establishes fundamental constraints on what properties of the stochastic process can be inferred from measured event counts alone. We illustrate these constraints in two biophysical examples: an activity-monitoring assay for a small organism based on detector crossings and population size estimation from encounter counts, in which we recover and generalize classical sensing limits. Our framework thus provides a unified theoretical description of counting processes driven by latent diffusion dynamics, and quantifies how much information each process carries about the other.

papers.title: A Diagrammatic Method for Non-Gaussian Photon Correlations in Weakly Coupled Atomic Ensembles
papers.summary: We develop a scattering-theory formalism and use it to predict that a resonantly driven atomic ensemble weakly coupled to an optical mode can generate light with non-Gaussian correlations. The temporal pattern of $g_c^{(3)}$ is explained using the microscopic transport processes in terms of our diagrams. We derive an optical-depth-dependent bound on the perturbative truncation error and benchmark our predictions against cascaded master-equation and quantum trajectory simulations for small ensembles with $\mathrm{OD}\leq 2$, identifying a regime of controlled accuracy under weak driving. Our predictions can be experimentally demonstrated in state-of-the-art nanofibre-coupled atomic ensembles.

papers.title: Separation-Dependent Bell Correlations from Prepared Coherence in Dirac Wavepackets
papers.summary: We calculate separation-dependent Bell correlations for a fixed pair of Dirac electron wavepackets in a free, weakly relativistic packet model, treating the prepared joint wave as a physical wave--entity. It occurs already at leading spin order, including for equal prepared branch weights. Interference between direct and exchanged assignments of the electron waves to the stations changes the relative weights and phases of the sampled spin amplitudes, thereby modulating the optimized response. Representative finite spatial and timing windows reduce visibility while retaining broader suppression and revival. This wave--entity account gives a quantitative, testable correlation pattern from prepared coherence, deterministic propagation, and local sampling, without postulating transmission between detectors.

papers.title: Symmetry breaking transforms strong to normal correlation and false metals to true insulators
papers.summary: Material scientists and condensed matter physicists have long been divided on the issue of choosing the conceptual framework for explaining why open-shell transition-metal oxides tend to be insulators, whereas otherwise successful theories such as DFT often predict them to be (false) metals. Strong correlation becomes the recommended medicine. We point out that strong correlation can be mitigated by allowing DFT to lower the energy by breaking structural, magnetic or dipolar symmetries. Such local motifs are observed experimentally by local probes beyond the 'average structure' determined by X-Ray diffraction. Observed broken symmetries can arise from slow fluctuations that persist over the observation time or longer. The surprising fact is that when symmetry breaking motifs are used as input to electronic structure calculations, false metals are converted into real insulators without the recommended medicine of strong correlation. Consistently, DFT calculations that show energy lowering symmetry breaking correct most cases where DFT, even with advanced exchange-correlation functionals, previously missed the correct metal vs insulator designation. Total energy calculations distinguish systems that support energy-lowering symmetry breaking from those that do not. This approach distinguishes between paramagnetic insulating and metallic phases and shows mass enhancement in Mott metals. The reason is that symmetry breaking removes many of the degeneracies that exist in a symmetry-unbroken system, reducing significantly the need for strong correlation. If one chooses to ignore symmetry breaking, the persistent degeneracies often call for strong correlation treatment. Thus, symmetry breaking transforms strong to normal correlation and false metals to true insulators. This view sheds light on the historic controversy between Mott and Slater that still reverberates today.

papers.title: Emergence and coexistence of periodic and unstructured motion in future-avoiding random walks
papers.summary: Self-avoiding random walks on graphs can be seen as walkers interacting with their own past history. Here, we consider a complementary class of dynamics, mutual future-avoiding random walks (MFARWs), where stochastically driven walkers are avoiding each other's planned future trajectories. Such systems arise naturally in conceptual models of shared mobility. We show that periodic behavior emerges spontaneously in two different MFARWs, and that periodic and unstructured behavior coexist, providing an example of chimera like behavior of nonoscillatory paths on networks. Further, we analytically describe and predict the onset of structure. We find that the transition from unstructured to periodic behavior is driven by a mechanism of self-amplifying coupling to the periodic components of the stochastic drivers of the system. In the context of shared mobility applications, these states imply a regime of naturally stable coexistence between flexible and line-based public transport.

papers.title: Determining G with Laser Spectroscopy to 38 ppb
papers.summary: A precision measurement is proposed to determine, in a couple hours of integration time, the axion Compton frequency using a modest power (3 mW) tunable external cavity diode laser at 2458 nm as input to drive a free space tabletop Mach Zehnder interferometer whose sensing arm passes the expanded beam waist (3 mm) light beam through a 1 T strong, 40 cm long dipole magnetic field created by a custom built permanent magnet assembly with a large but achievable (6 mm) gap between poles. As the laser frequency is slowly modulated at 1 kHz through a 600 MHz wide window that is well within the 30 GHz fine tuning range of the laser, a small but readily observable modulation appears in the dark port optical power of the dark fringe phase locked interferometer due to photons converting into axions within the light beam as it passes through the magnetic field. Measuring the axion Compton frequency, around 122 THz, where the dark port power modulation peaks, to within the linewidth of the laser, about 1 MHz, then determines G to 38 parts per billion (ppb), a roughly 600 fold improvement, through a relation between the axion Compton frequency and G, involving h, c, and nucleon masses.

papers.title: Nonlinear Dynamics of Rapidly Driven Systems

The general structure of the high-frequency expansion reveals a broad class of nonlinear systems whose transition curves are identical to those of the linear Mathieu equation, which enables a fully nonperturbative stability analysis in the case of strong driving and nonlinearity. The method is generalized to velocity-dependent forces and configuration space with curvature, characteristic to systems with constraints. Several applications are discussed in detail, including the dynamical magnetic trapping of electric charges.

papers.title: Ultra-long simulations of collisionless relativistic shocks in front-comoving frame: evidence for a steady state and its properties
papers.summary: We present a series of unprecedently long 2D3V PIC simulations of unmagnetized relativistic $e^{-}e^{+}$-pair shocks performed in a front-comoving frame. By implementing a moving-wall boundary condition in the downstream together with continuous injection at the upstream boundary, we maintain a fixed simulation domain size, opening the way to perform substantially longer simulations. Our longest runs extend beyond $100000\,\omega_p^{-1}$, exceeding the duration of the previously published simulations by a factor of several. Across a diverse set of simulations --- varying upstream/downstream lengths, transverse sizes, and particle-per-cell counts --- we find strong evidence that the shock, {modelled for a long-time in the front-comoving frame,} approaches an asymptotic, time-independent state. In the downstream region, the steady state depends only on the upstream temperature at the injection boundary and {remains the same if we change the downstream and upstream lengths.} The upstream precursor evolves slower and retains a dependence on the simulation's upstream length, that may be of minor observational consequence, since radiation from astrophysical shocks predominantly originates from the downstream region. {Our simulations also indicate} that Fermi-type acceleration is limited in energy and a true power-law tail never forms. Another important finding is that the downstream magnetic field has a soliton-like structure, where individual magnetic domains evolve independently, each comprising a compact, highly magnetized core embedded within an extended, weakly magnetized region. The magnetic-field distribution around the centers of these spots has approximately Lorentzian profile.

papers.title: PASS: Perturbation augmented space group structure sampling for transferable Fe-O machine learning interatomic potential
papers.summary: Iron (Fe) oxidation is a fundamental phenomenon that is scientifically vital and technologically significant. Despite substantial experimental efforts, accurate atomistic modelling of Fe oxidation remains elusive, which requires a reliable interatomic potential, whose development hinges on a representative first-principles training dataset. However, Fe-oxygen (O) system is known for its structural complexity, rendering the generation of high-quality first-principles dataset challenging. In this work, we propose the Perturbation Augmented Space group structure Sampling (PASS) method to generate extensive dataset for Fe-O system consisting of small-cell structures (no more than 10 atoms). Based on atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework, we present a systematic approach to developing a transferable machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The accuracy and capability of the ACE potential are thoroughly validated across pure Fe and Fe-O systems through bulk, surface, and interface properties. The large-scale Fe oxidation simulations with the ACE potential capture key features of the oxidation process, including the formation of an FeO-like structure consistent with recent experimental observations. This work demonstrates that the PASS method yields an accurate and transferable MLIP that can capture the reactive complexity of oxide growth while remaining computationally practical for extended systems.

papers.title: When more data become less informative: Finite-precision periodicization and collapse of forecast-error Lyapunov estimates
papers.summary: Equation-free forecast-error analysis is useful when governing equations, Jacobians, tangent dynamics, or full state vectors are unavailable and only scalar time series are observed. In this setting, the multi-horizon forecast-error curve can provide both an instability estimate and nonlinear predictive features, making its numerical reliability important. We show that long finite-precision chaotic records can enter an information-saturation regime in which increasing record length N (the total number of analyzed samples) adds repeated histories rather than new dynamical information. For the float32 logistic map, exact recurrence progressively fills the training catalogue with duplicate histories and identical futures, suppressing forecast-error growth and driving the estimated Lyapunov slope toward zero. Across 10,000 initial conditions, exact recurrence occurred by iteration 7612; across 28 stratified seeds, collapse onset strongly followed the recurrence-occupancy scale. A two-dimensional H\'enon-map control confirms that recurrence and estimator failure are separate events: the float32 trajectory enters an exact machine-state cycle after a transient of $\mu = 103,039$ samples, with cycle period P = 12,268, yet the forecast-error estimate remains close to the positive Jacobian/QR reference until catalogue saturation near N = 200,000. Casting an already generated float32 record to float64 does not restore lost information, whereas genuine float64 generation, restarted short trajectories, and one-ULP perturbations prevent collapse over the tested range. A recursive local-linear predictor exhibits the same endpoint at a later, predictor-dependent threshold. The results identify a recurrence-to-catalogue-saturation failure mode specific to forecast-error/analogue inference rather than Lyapunov estimation in general.

papers.title: Optimizing GEDI Simulator Configuration for European Temperate Forests
papers.summary: Accurate estimation of aboveground biomass density is essential for quantifying forest carbon stocks. NASA's GEDI mission provides valuable canopy structure data, but its sparse sampling necessitates the use of simulators to calibrate biomass models at field inventory locations. The widely used simulator of Hancock et al. (2019) emulates GEDI waveforms from airborne LiDAR point clouds, yet it has never been validated over European temperate forests. Here, we compare approximately 8,100 pairs of observed and simulated GEDI relative height (RH) profiles across French forests using the national airborne LiDAR program as input. We separate two sources of error: waveform modeling differences, assessed by referencing both simulated and real RH metrics to a common ALS-derived ground elevation, and ground detection bias, evaluated by comparing each GEDI L2A processing algorithm against the ALS reference. Under the baseline configuration, the mean absolute bias across the full RH profile reaches 0.67 m in leaf-on and 1.20 m in leaf-off conditions. Switching to intensity-based return weighting and selecting the a3 L2A algorithm reduces these biases to 0.43 m and 0.42 m respectively. The a3 algorithm also achieves near-unbiased ground detection (+0.04 m versus -0.82 m for the default), directly reducing a previously overlooked source of error. We also show that leaf-off acquisitions and low-sensitivity shots, both typically excluded from standard biomass products, are simulated as reliably as their counterparts, substantially expanding the potential calibration and inference datasets.

papers.title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
papers.summary: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.

papers.title: Making Weak Interlayer Excitons Absorb: Manipulating the Effective Oscillator Strength via Purcell Engineering of Critical Coupling
papers.summary: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. However, the large electron-hole separation underlying their dipolar character also results in a significantly reduced oscillator strength, limiting their direct optical interaction with light, and thus the direct probing of their dynamics and many-body interactions. Here, we show that by using Purcell engineering of critical coupling, a weak interlayer transition can absorb as strongly as the dominant intralayer transition, despite its much smaller intrinsic oscillator strength. Using this approach, in an open cavity architecture we demonstrate an order of magnitude IX absorption modulation in bilayer and trilayer MoS2, with doubling of the IX to A-exciton interaction strength weight from ~23% to ~53%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a tailored closed cavity architecture, the IX enhancement can reach beyond an order of magnitude, from ~5% to ~83% excitonic absorption, enabling IX absorption similar to intralayer excitons. An analytical description of the interaction is obtained via a closed-form transmission-line model which separates the excitonic and photonic contributions to the optical response, revealing how cavity architecture can be designed towards critical coupling. Our findings establish Purcell engineering of critical coupling as a general route to controlling and enhancing weak excitonic transitions.

papers.title: Curved Monopoles and Yagi-Uda Arrays for Low-Angle HF Skywave Radiation over Lossy Ground: Analysis, Hybrid Bayesian Optimization, and Validated Full-Wave Design
papers.summary: High-frequency (HF) skywave radars require high gain at take-off angles of 3 degrees-30 degrees, where vertically polarized monopoles and Yagi-Uda arrays over lossy land suffer from pseudo-Brewster cancellation. This paper shows that curving the elements of HF monopoles and Yagi-Uda arrays converts radiation from this soil-limited transverse-magnetic route into a transverse-electric route that is nearly insensitive to soil conditions. Closed-form half-space bounds quantify both routes and yield design rules; a separability result extends the soil insensitivity to arrays. A hybrid design method combines Bayesian optimization on analytical and method-of-moments models with full-wave simulations of a screened site on moist soil; current extraction differs by at most 5.1% RMS, and Fresnel post-processing agrees with independent perfect-ground results within 0.16 dB in pointwise gain for four arrays. At 15 MHz, a self-matched 2-element curved Yagi-Uda array and a Bayesian-optimized 3-element array achieve realized forward-sector gains of 6.8 and 8.3 dBi over moist soil, 6.4 and 6.3 dB above straight quarter-wave Yagi-Uda arrays optimized by the same procedure, with 92%-95% efficiency. Their gain changes by about 1 dB from a perfect ground to very dry soil, whereas that of the straight arrays falls by 9 dB. Bayesian optimization, confirmed by full-wave simulation, identified a design 0.2 dB above the sweep optimum and a gain-bandwidth Pareto front that offers up to twice the matched bandwidth. The results also show that the native far field of full-wave solvers can overestimate the low-angle gain of vertical arrays over soil by more than 4 dB.

papers.title: Matter that learns what matters
papers.summary: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show this in a model optical network, where action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. A reduced stochastic model, calibrated retrospectively from local response statistics, accounts for changes in sequence completion across writing rules without fitting the aggregate success rates. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.

papers.title: Where Does the Anion-Redox Hole Go? Reliability of Open-Shell Projection-Based Embedding for Li-Rich Cathodes, from DFT Environments to Quantum Solvers
papers.summary: Anion redox in Li-rich layered oxides places holes on oxygen next to an antiferromagnetic Mn(IV) d3 lattice, a strongly correlated open-shell problem for which projection-based wavefunction-in-DFT embedding offers a route to correlated and quantum solvers, but whose errors are known mainly for closed-shell molecules. We develop a spin-unrestricted projection-based embedding, exact at the DFT-in-DFT level to the microhartree scale for closed-shell, broken-symmetry and high-spin references with point charges, and apply DMRG-in-DFT to point-charge clusters of delithiated Li(2-x)MnO3, varying the environment functional (0-100% exact exchange), geometry, active region, active-space spin, virtual space, cluster size and magnetic reference. In every setting the lowest SCF state places the hole on an oxygen pair, with no O-O bond. How the hole is shared depends on the functional together with the geometry: hybrids give a full, uncoupled hole at the DFT+U geometry but a partial, weakly covalent hole at their own geometry, a change of up to 0.5 e on one oxygen. Where spin spreads across the active/environment boundary, the integer spin projection of the active space becomes a choice worth up to 0.26 e, and at most 0.09 e once the two Mn neighbors are included. An extended state search found missed lower states for two functionals, changing a pair-oxygen spin by up to 0.45 e. Across all 82 runs the embedded mean field gives the same hole (median DMRG change 0.02-0.04 e); correlation mainly adds O-O covalency. State control and geometry consistency, not the solver, dominate the uncertainty, and total energies are not converged at 30-40 orbitals. For quantum solvers, the embedded Hamiltonian must be spin-unrestricted: a shared-orbital form reverses the hole, while sample-based quantum diagonalization reproduces exact diagonalization, as accurately as, but not better than, classical selected CI.

papers.title: The Mean First-Reaction Time on a Thin Filament in a 3-D Domain
papers.summary: We study the mean first-reaction time (MFRT) of a Brownian particle in a bounded three-dimensional domain $\Omega$ with a reflecting boundary $\partial\Omega$, that contains a thin reactive filament. The filament is a tube of cross-sectional diameter $\varepsilon\ll 1$ around a smooth closed curve $\Gamma$, and its surface is partially reactive with reactivity $b$. As $\varepsilon\to 0$ the filament reduces to a line source in the outer problem. Its cross-section enters only through a logarithmic reactive capacitance $d_c(b)$, so that the MFRT is O$(-\log[\varepsilon d_c])$. This contrasts with the $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ scaling for spatially localized traps of radius $\varepsilon$. Using matched asymptotic expansions, we derive a Fredholm integral equation on $\Gamma$ for the line density of the reactive flux. It sums all powers of $\nu\equiv -1/\log[\varepsilon d_c]$ and involves two geometric quantities: the regular part $R$ of the Neumann Green's function, which encodes the interaction of $\Gamma$ with $\partial\Omega$, and an intrinsic self-energy of $\Gamma$ that depends only on its shape. The framework extends to multiple filaments, splitting probabilities, a spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, and the principal eigenvalue of the Laplacian. For the unit sphere we solve the integral equation with a simple trapezoidal Nystr\"om scheme, and we validate the predictions for rings, linked rings and torus knots against full 3-D finite-element solutions.

papers.title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
papers.summary: While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among the leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.

papers.title: Quantum Cosmology at the Cusp
papers.summary: In top-down quantum gravity constructions, saxionic directions typically lead to cusps in moduli space, where the scalar potential and the axion decay constant asymptotically behave as $V\sim e^{-\alpha\phi}$ and $f\sim e^{-\gamma\phi}$ in reduced Planck units. Such cusps admit axion-supported scaling cosmologies that expand faster than the corresponding solutions with the axion held fixed, for the same scalar potential. In spatially compact universes, axionic momentum is quantized, and any semiclassical state in the cusp with a localized axion carries nonzero axionic kinetic energy. We show using the Wheeler-DeWitt equation that this contribution drives the late-time evolution towards the axion-supported scaling solution whenever $(d-2)\alpha(\alpha+2\gamma)>4(d-1)$ in $d$ spacetime dimensions. We derive an upper bound on the transition time. Long-lived accelerated expansion requires $2\gamma>(d-2)\alpha$. The trans-Planckian censorship conjecture requires the opposite inequality, $2\gamma\leq(d-2)\alpha$, which also follows independently from requiring the brane magnetically charged under the axion to remain heavier than the Hubble scale.

papers.title: Guaranteed Slater Conditions for the Numerical Conformal Bootstrap: Fixing Instabilities in SDPB, Navigator Methods, and Skydiving
papers.summary: The semidefinite programs (SDPs) of the numerical conformal bootstrap, and of S-matrix and quantum-mechanics bootstraps, are solved with primal-dual interior-point methods whose convergence guarantees rest on primal and dual Slater conditions: the existence of strictly feasible points on both sides of the duality. Many bootstrap SDPs violate these. The consequences range from slow convergence to inconclusive verdicts and the breakdown of the Skydive algorithm. We introduce "Slater tools", all acting within the PMP class accepted by SDPB. Diagnostics measure the Slater margins and, when a margin vanishes, extract the exposing certificate that identifies the degeneracy. Two independent cures follow. Transforms that provide rigorous bounds on the original SDP objective and that for the right parameter choices return the exact value. Facial reductions that use the exposing certificate to remove the degeneracies themselves. We reproduce, explain and resolve all known types of failures in a mixed-correlator 3d Ising setup. We show that the $X$-Slater condition (SDPB's primal) fails at every disallowed point in feasibility mode, holds in every navigator problem we tested, and can be guaranteed by one additional condition on the navigator function. We show that the folklore "instability remedy" of a twist gap works by removing degeneracies at the endpoints of the positivity conditions. These often stem from a mistake in factoring out the block prefactor but can also arise legitimately in channels that mix equal and unequal operator pairs. Finally we classify and remove all degeneracies of the published current-scalar bootstrap, among them one at $x=\infty$, thus incurable by any gap assumption, caused by unequal polynomial degrees within one matrix block.

papers.title: The running of Weyl gauged gravity: asymptotic freedom, its obstruction, and a way out
papers.summary: We compute the one-loop beta functions of quadratic gravity in Weyl conformal geometry, the gauge theory of diffeomorphisms and dilatations with a dynamical Weyl gauge boson. The divergences are extracted diagrammatically in the background field method, with a gauge fixing procedure adapted to the semidirect product structure of the gauge group. The Weyl-tensor coupling and the Weyl gauge coupling are asymptotically free, and the running of the latter is special, being independent of the other couplings and of any two-derivative matter content. The obstruction to an ultraviolet completion comes from the square of a Weyl-covariant curvature scalar, denoted $\widehat{R}{}^2$: the flow of the corresponding coupling has no fixed point in the physically interesting region and becomes trivial, the only real fixed points require a decoupled Weyl boson and a tachyonic scalar mode. This also holds when including the Standard Model with any nonminimal Higgs coupling and, more generally, for any matter with two-derivative kinetic terms. Weyl-invariant four-derivative scalars with a sufficiently large coupling to $\widehat{R}{}^2$ can remove the obstruction, producing a fixed point in the physical region that is ultraviolet attractive in all directions and has a nonvanishing Weyl gauge coupling.

papers.title: DiscKosky: Efficient Genealogical Constraints from Sector-By-Sector Critical Point Counting
papers.summary: We present DiscKosky, a new Mathematica package for efficiently generating genealogical constraints on the sequential discontinuities of Feynman integrals. DiscKosky works by tracking the solutions to the critical point equations associated with a Feynman integral; by identifying which of these critical points cease to exist in a given kinematic limit, we can associate each Landau singularity with a set of on-shell sectors. The hierarchical principle then forbids sequential discontinuities with respect to singularities that are associated with incompatible sets of on-shell propagators. In rare cases, this algorithm fails to make predictions due to the appearance of higher-dimensional critical varieties---nevertheless, we show that this phenomenon can sometimes be used to identify non-repeating discontinuities, which can be computed at most once in a Feynman integral. We illustrate the power of DiscKosky by applying the package to a broad class of Feynman integrals, including two-loop five-point integrals with one and two massive legs, and three-loop examples that go beyond the current computational frontier. DiscKosky can also be used to probe the analytic properties of more general classes of Euler integrals, which we illustrate by considering several examples that arise in the context of cosmological correlators.

papers.title: On Boundary State Screening via Solitons
papers.summary: We present a coarse classification scheme for the boundary data of massive QFTs based on transitions of boundary states via soliton / kink profiles. Starting from the lattice of boundary states, we introduce the boundary screening group $\mathbb{B}$: the equivalence classes of boundary states which cannot be connected by such transitions. In string theory backgrounds which geometrically engineer an interacting QFT in the target space, $\mathbb{B}$ computes the worldsheet analog of the target space defect group $\mathbb{D}$. When $\mathbb{B}$ is non-zero, it provides a diagnostic for having a target space with non-normalizable modes. For interfaces between QFTs, similar considerations imply the existence of a non-trivial conserved charge associated with soliton absorption / transmission, which means that the interface cannot fully dissolve / disappear. Similar considerations hold for junctions of QFTs, which in the special case of string worldsheet CFTs translate to junctions of string theories. We illustrate these general considerations with a number of non-geometric 2D $\mathcal{N} = (2,2)$ Landau-Ginzburg models, as well as their natural lifts to 4D $\mathcal{N} = 1$ Wess-Zumino models.
