papers.title: Learning from Expert-Corrected Misdiagnoses: A Self-Evolving Consultation Agent for Traditional Chinese Medicine after Failed Treatment
papers.summary: In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), treatment follows syndrome differentiation (bianzheng), the step that maps a patient's findings to a TCM syndrome. A misdiagnosed syndrome therefore leads directly to inappropriate treatment, and the error usually surfaces only after that treatment fails. The physician who sees the patient next must diagnose a condition already altered by the wrong therapy, identify the initial physician's error, and avoid continuing the failed therapeutic direction. We introduce TCM-MisDx, an interactive benchmark of 820 consultations after treatment failure built from three published monographs of TCM misdiagnosis cases. An agent gathers symptoms, tongue and pulse findings through the four diagnostic methods before reporting the current syndrome, the initial error, and a corrective treatment plan. We further present TCM-SEA, a self-evolving consultation agent that rewrites its own clinical skill document: failed consultations are compared with the expert physician's documented analysis, the agent proposes a minimal edit, and the edit is kept only if it passes an acceptance gate on held-in and held-out cases. The underlying language model is never updated. On the sealed test set, TCM-SEA raises the composite score from 61.8 to 65.5, syndrome accuracy from 53.9 to 57.2 and treatment-principle accuracy from 44.7 to 48.9, and lowers the therapeutic momentum rate, the fraction of corrective plans that keep the initial physician's failed direction, from 44.1 to 38.2. Learning from expert cases outperforms learning from outcome feedback alone, with the largest gains on the monograph of inappropriate-treatment cases. The two accepted edits are short, human-readable clinical checklists that physicians can audit directly.

papers.title: Physics-Grounded Simulation Enables Zero-Shot Molecular and Reaction Analysis in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy
papers.summary: Quantitative identification of molecular products and reaction pathways from scanning tunneling microscopy images is difficult when labeled images are unavailable for a new chemical system. We develop a simulation-assisted framework for zero-shot analysis that requires only precursor information for a new target system, with no experimental images or annotations from that system used during model training. The framework couples two functional components: NanoSim generates physics-grounded synthetic images from predicted reaction products and sampled surface scenes, while NanoAnalysis translates molecular detections into product populations, spatial arrangements, and mechanistic interpretations. Applied to a representative on-surface reaction, the detector achieves a micro-averaged F1 score of 0.92 on experimental images. Analysis of the detected molecules reveals annealing-dependent population changes and reaction-site preferences consistent with experimental observations. Beyond this capability, its modular organization allows heterogeneous data from other systems to be used to improve each component independently, providing a scalable route for continued generalization.

papers.title: Tree-based Algorithms for Breakpoint Median and Near-Median Genomes
papers.summary: Median genomes serve as candidates for ancestral reconstruction and help study the diversity of parsimonious rearrangement solutions. However, the breakpoint median problem is NP-hard for unichromosomal genomes, and medians are non-unique, making their diversity important to study. In this paper, we develop tree-based algorithms for studying breakpoint medians of linear unichromosomal genomes represented as unsigned permutations. The algorithms construct rooted labeled trees whose leaves encode candidate median genomes satisfying local adjacency constraints derived from the inputs. We show that the resulting reduced search spaces contain all breakpoint medians while being much smaller than the full permutation space. We investigate these reduced spaces experimentally for three-genome instances. Our method finds exact medians and many near-optimal approximations, while early sampling of leaves often produces near-medians quickly. We also introduce constrained sampling procedures for targeting balanced near-medians, whose distances to the input genomes are more evenly distributed and hence are particularly relevant for ancestral reconstruction. The resulting framework provides a unified method for exact enumeration, efficient sampling, and targeted exploration of median and near-median genomes. In contrast to Traveling Salesman Problem-based approaches, which typically return a single solution and do not reveal the diversity or balance of the median set, our method can enumerate all medians, sample near-medians early, and target structurally distinct candidates under the breakpoint distance.

papers.title: Expression of White and Gray Matter Autism Functional Network Connectivity Signatures in Infancy
papers.summary: Functional connectivity studies have provided valuable insights into altered brain organization in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, most functional connectivity studies focus exclusively on either gray matter (GM) regions or white matter (WM) tracts and examine specific age groups, rather than investigating their functional interactions across brain development. This limits our understanding of how GM-WM functional interactions evolve developmentally and may obscure important aspects of brain network organization in ASD. We combined integrated WM+GM functional network connectivity (FNC) with brain-wide risk scores (BRSs) to quantify ASD-associated pattern expression in ABIDE I/II and an independent infant cohort. We employed a NeuroMark framework with predefined WM and GM intrinsic connectivity networks templates, to estimate subject-level FNC. First, we identified two distinct patterns of altered WM+GM FNC in ASD: GM-related hypoconnectivity centered on the paralimbic network and WM-GM hyperconnectivity centered on the frontal network. These findings highlight the involvement of higher-order cognitive networks and the importance of WM-GM functional interactions in characterizing ASD-related connectivity alterations. Second, infants with a higher familial likelihood of autism exhibited greater mean expression of ASD-associated FNC patterns than those with a lower familial likelihood, as quantified by BRS. These group-level findings do not establish developmental persistence or predict diagnostic outcomes at the individual level.

papers.title: Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations
papers.summary: Summary statistics that measure the shapes of phylogenetic trees contributed to quantitatively understanding evolutionary processes. Among phylogenetic summary statistics, the tree balance indices have been designed to capture intuitive notions of balance or imbalance in trees. Here, we characterize the tree balance indices in terms of basis statistics, mapping the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces. We observe that many tree balance indices can be represented in terms of linear functions of these low-dimensional spaces, enabling us to compute exact formulas for the means, variances, and covariances of many balance indices under the Yule--Harding model. The new framework recapitulates existing formulas for the expectations of 8 indices: Sackin index, average leaf depth, total cophenetic index, $\hat{s}$-shape statistic, Colless index, corrected Colless index, quadratic Colless index, and rooted quartet index for binary trees. It produces new formulas for the expectations of 9 additional indices: equal weights Colless index, total $I$ index, total $I'$ index, Rogers $J$ index, total internal path length, total path length, average vertex depth, stairs1 index, and stairs2 index. Moreover, the framework also allows us to calculate the exact variance of all 17 indices that are represented by the bases as well as the covariance and correlation for all $\binom{17}{2} = 136$ pairs among the 17 indices.

papers.title: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running
papers.summary: Rhythmic behaviours such as walking and running are commonly modelled as dynamical systems around a stable limit cycle. To keep such models tractable, it is usually assumed that each step depends only on the previous one, that the limit cycle is fixed, and that the sagittal and frontal planes can be studied separately. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.

papers.title: Contribution of chromosome-na\"ive transposon-seeded network of DNA templates to intracellular pools of protein dimers of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensate-forming proteins
papers.summary: Molecular mechanisms governing protein-protein interactions (PPI) contributing to the biogenesis of membraneless condensates remain poorly understood. Observations reported in this contribution demonstrate that liquid-liquid phase-separated (LLPS) condensate-forming proteins and their variants harboring condensate-disrupting human pathogenic mutations are significantly enriched among PPI cascade constituents of the Hybrid Assembly Pathway (HAP) of endogenous multiprotein complexes (EMC). In contrast, no structured or disordered proteins defined as condensate-negative molecules were detected among PPI cascade constituents. Cumulative evidence derived from different lines of analytical inquiries support the concept of the significant contributions of PPI cascade constituents of HAP to the biogenesis of intracellular pools of cell type-specific protein heterodimers assembled with the engagement of at least one protein monomer selected from condensate-forming protein molecules. Analytical evidence documented in this study support the concept that genome-wide chromosome-na\"ive networks of transposon-seeded DNA-templates nucleate the initiation of PPI cascade chain reactions with the capacity to facilitate the concurrent iterative assembly in human cells of both the membraneless biomolecular condensates and the structured multiprotein complexes. AlphaFold 3D modelling of mutation patterns and analysis of partner-bound experimental structures identified variants located at a measured protein dimerization interface. This contribution nominates numerous protein heterodimers of potential relevance to human pathophysiology for follow-up mechanistic studies of potential fundamental and translational impacts.

papers.title: An extension of the classic Buneman theorem from phylogenetic trees to networks
papers.summary: Phylogenetic networks provide a natural framework for representing reticulate evolutionary events such as horizontal gene transfer and hybridization. In the present manuscript, we investigate the identifiability of phylogenetic networks under (hardwired) parsimony, a natural extension of Maximum Parsimony from trees to networks. More precisely, we ask which structural features of a network can be uniquely inferred from so-called $A_k$-alignments under this criterion. While identifiability has been studied extensively for phylogenetic trees under parsimony, little is known about the identifiability of networks under hardwired parsimony. We take a first step towards addressing this gap by developing a general framework for studying identifiability under hardwired parsimony. We then use this framework to show that the tree of blobs of a phylogenetic network can be reconstructed from its $A_1$-alignment. This result can be viewed as a natural extension of Buneman's well-known splits equivalence theorem. Finally, we show that, under hardwired parsimony, cycles of length at least $5$ cannot in general be uniquely identified from character data, establishing a fundamental limitation of hardwired parsimony.

papers.title: Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics
papers.summary: We introduce a unified optimal transport framework for the Immersed Boundary (IB) electrodiffusion active pump model. By representing membrane chemical potential barriers and active pump potentials via smoothed Eulerian kernels ($\Psi_w, \mathcal{H}_w$), we formulate the passive dynamics as an $L^2$-Wasserstein ($W_2$) gradient flow coupled to non-conservative active pushing fields representing ATP-driven $3:2$ $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ exchangers. We establish global weak existence of solutions to the continuous Poisson--Nernst--Planck--IB system via a split-step Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) variational scheme, backed by Calder\'on--Zygmund bounds for non-local Poisson drift and $H^3(\mathbb{S}^1)$ interface regularity under Stokes flow. We prove the continuous Rayleighian energy balance and establish exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS) under a quantitative Bakry--\'Emery curvature threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the dual singular limits of kernel smoothing width $w \to 0$ and dimensionless Debye length $g = \lambda_D / L \to 0$. We establish the precise asymptotic regime connecting regularized and sharp models, prove the $\Gamma$-convergence of regularized energy functionals, derive distributional interface flux jump conditions, and resolve $O(\lambda_D)$ Debye space-charge boundary layers to confirm bulk electroneutrality.

papers.title: Genetic weight of a mutant in a biparental Moran model with infinite selection
papers.summary: We study, after Coron Le Jan (2024), the genetic contribution of a single strongly advantageous mutant in a biparental Moran model under infinite selection. We prove a functional limit theorem for the entire beneficial mutation spreading period: after normalization by \(\sqrt N\), the contributions carried by the advantaged and disadvantaged subpopulations converge jointly in law to a non-degenerate random multiple of an explicit deterministic profile. Randomness is generated during the initial microscopic growth of the mutant lineage and subsequently propagated through the population along a deterministic macroscopic trajectory. At the heart of this phenomenon is an eigenmode martingale that measures the imbalance between the mean genetic weight of the founding ancestor within the two classes; its limiting value provides precisely the random amplitude of the macroscopic profile and is characterized by a smoothing equation.

papers.title: A two-stage diffusion-driven morphogenesis model with evolving connectivity
papers.summary: Morphogenesis of diatom silica shells involves a sequence of topological transitions: initially separate ribs grow and branch, then merge through bridges, leaving a regular network of pores. Existing models based on diffusion-limited aggregation or reaction-diffusion reproduce either branching or pore formation, but not both within a single framework. Here we propose a two-stage model of diffusion-driven morphogenesis with evolving connectivity. The model is formulated on a fixed finite element mesh with a density field on an active layer. Stage 1 reproduces dendritic growth, where a stimulus based on the local diffusive flux exceeds a threshold. Stage 2 uses an inverted stimulus, where high local flux suppresses precipitation, stabilizing pores between the dendrites. The update rules are analogous to sensitivity in density-based topology optimization and to strain energy density in bone remodeling. The model predicts distinct morphological regimes on each stage, controlled by the respective thresholds. For a reference calculation, the predicted pore network is regular, with approximately uniform spacing, and pores are absent near the domain edges, consistent with observations on diatom valves. The model provides a unified framework for describing both stages of silica morphogenesis and suggests a route for comparing computational predictions with cryo-electron tomography data.

papers.title: Nonequilibrium Transient Centers in Continuous-Time Systems
papers.summary: Analysis of mathematical models in ecology and epidemiology often emphasizes asymptotic dynamics, such as stable equilibria, periodic orbits, and attractors. However, many biologically relevant trajectories exhibit long transient dynamics in which a relevant observable evolves slowly for an extended period before a comparatively rapid transition occurs. On finite time scales relevant to data collection, management, and intervention, such transient behavior can be more informative than the eventual asymptotic outcome. In this work, we study long-lasting and slowly varying transient dynamics in continuous-time systems through the framework of nonequilibrium transient centers. These centers are points in the state space near which the observable can remain nearly constant for a long time, even when the full state is not near an equilibrium. We develop finite-time escape criteria for identifying such centers and their reachable counterparts. These criteria provide practical conditions under which nearby trajectories can remain in a slow regime for a long period of time before eventually leaving it. We apply the theory to an epidemic model with delay of stability loss. In this model, trajectories may remain close to the disease-free manifold for a long time before the infectious population resurges. The framework developed here describes this behavior as slow evolution near a nonequilibrium transient center followed by finite-time escape from the slow regime.

papers.title: Les Houches Lectures on Community Ecology: From Niche Theory to Statistical Mechanics
papers.summary: Ecosystems are among the most interesting and well-studied examples of self-organized complex systems. Community ecology, the study of how species interact with each other and the environment, has a rich tradition. Over the last few years, there has been a growing theoretical and experimental interest in these problems from the physics and quantitative biology communities. Here, we give an overview of community ecology, highlighting the deep connections between ecology and statistical physics. We start by introducing the two classes of mathematical models that have served as the workhorses of community ecology: Consumer Resource Models (CRM) and the generalized Lotka-Volterra models (GLV). We place a special emphasis on graphical methods and general principles. We then review recent works showing a deep and surprising connection between ecological dynamics and constrained optimization. We then shift our focus by analyzing these same models in "high-dimensions" (i.e. in the limit where the number of species and resources in the ecosystem becomes large) and discuss how such complex ecosystems can be analyzed using methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems such as the cavity method and Random Matrix Theory.

papers.title: Explainable AI-Driven Neural Activity Analysis in Parkinsonian Rats under Electrical Stimulation
papers.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor dysfunction and abnormal neural oscillations. This study combined graphene-based cortical stimulation with an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework to investigate spatial and frequency-related features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals were recorded before and after stimulation and classified using EEGNet and DeepConvNet. Layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) and DeepLIFT were applied to identify frequency bands and recording channels contributing to the classification. The anatomical locations of these channels were mapped onto a cortical map. XAI analyses were performed separately for each animal to examine individual attribution patterns. Our XAI analysis revealed frequency-band- and region-specific contributions to pre- and post-stimulation classification in Parkinsonian rats. Our approach provided complementary insights into the features contributing to pre- and post-stimulation ECoG classification alongside PSD-based analyses. These findings highlight the potential of combining graphene-based cortical stimulation with explainable deep learning to identify classification-relevant features across frequency bands and cortical areas in pre- and post-stimulation recordings.

papers.title: Building functional and mechanistic models of cortical computation based on canonical cell type connectivity
papers.summary: Neuronal circuits of the cerebral cortex are the structural basis of mammalian cognition. The same qualitative components and connectivity motifs are repeated across functionally specialized cortical areas and mammalian species, suggesting a single underlying algorithmic motif. Here, we propose a perspective on current knowledge of the cortical structure, from which we extract two core principles for computational modeling. The first principle is that cortical cell types fulfill distinct computational roles. The second principle is that cortical connectivity can be efficiently characterized by only a few canonical blueprints of connectivity between cell types. Starting with these two foundational principles, we outline a general framework for building functional and mechanistic models of cortical circuits. Finally, we show that the compressed and generative representations of connectivity entailed by this framework are particularly amenable to automatic search through gradient-free optimization, providing a concrete first step towards modelling the evolution of functional neural circuits.

papers.title: Message interaction dynamics covary with brain volume across mammalian connectomes
papers.summary: Brain network communication models typically assume that signals propagate independently, despite the high network density and small diameter of mammalian connectomes, where interactions among simultaneously propagating messages are likely. We investigate these interactions using the copy-spread-annihilate (CSA) model, a synchronous Markovian message-passing process in which messages spread through the binarized network while undergoing collision-dependent deletion. Simulations on a large comparative dataset of mammalian connectomes show that CSA dynamics produce robust positively-skewed lognormal distributions of message survival across species. Despite using only binary network topology without spatial embedding, message survival accounts for over half of the variance in brain volume across mammal species and outperforms a broad range of established graph-theoretic measures and an alternative communication model with interacting messages. These relationships persisted when measured paths could not revisit nodes. Degree-preserving switch randomization weakens the relationship between message survival and brain volume, indicating that higher-order structural organization contributes to the observed scaling law. We describe a mechanistic explanation of model dynamics that suggests message creation differences among networks shapes message survival. Together, these findings suggest that interactions among propagating messages constitute an important and underexplored determinant of communication dynamics in mammalian brain networks.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Navigation in Static and Dynamic Environments with Dual-Timescale Neuron-Astrocyte Memory
papers.summary: Biological agents navigate complex environments by combining long-term memory of successful actions with short-term suppression of recently visited locations-a capability difficult to replicate in artificial systems. We introduce a neuromorphic navigation system based on a spiking neuron--astrocyte network (SNAN), in which spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) reinforces traversed action sequences on a long timescale, while astrocytic calcium transients suppress moves into recently visited states on a short timescale. This dual-timescale memory biases the agent toward unexplored regions without reward signals or explicit global statistics. In grid worlds where the agent observes only its current position, astrocytic modulation increased goal completion from 45.9% to 99.9% and shortened median routes 5.8-15-fold on commonly solved tasks. Compared with seven classical strategies, including Tremaux's and Tarry's algorithms and tabular Q-learning, SNAN yields the shortest routes among reliable strategies in open and sparse static mazes while storing 2.8-4.6 times fewer variables than memory-based baselines. In dynamic mazes, its decaying memory retains no obsolete passage marks, so SNAN becomes more efficient as the topology changes. After ten learning cycles, STDP makes SNAN the best reliable strategy. The astrocytic modulation mitigates the exploration-exploitation trade-off through local state suppression, a form of working memory we term Topological-Context Memory. To validate hardware feasibility, we map STDP to a memristive VTEAM model and implement a subset of the network on a crossbar array, achieving order-of-magnitude gains in speed per area and energy per decision over CPU implementations. These results establish astrocyte-inspired dual-timescale memory as a compact, hardware-compatible principle for neuromorphic navigation.

papers.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space
papers.summary: Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes' vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin's own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line's effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin's data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2--4% of a near-vertical line's slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields' signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin's (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.

papers.title: Critical Flicker Fusion Frequency As An Experience-Restricted Constraint On Visual Temporal Resolution: What Does And Does Not Change It
papers.summary: Experience-dependent plasticity is fundamental to adaptive behaviour, yet the conditions under which basic sensory timing can be modified in adulthood remain poorly specified. Critical flicker fusion frequency (CFFF), the threshold at which flicker is perceived as continuous, is unusually informative here: what fails to change it is as well documented as what does. We argue that CFFF is best characterised neither as non-plastic nor as held near a physiological ceiling, but as modifiable only by a specific class of experience, not by amount. Repeated testing changes it little, and cognitive training without temporal content and incoherent-motion exposure leave it unchanged regardless of duration. By contrast, perceptual-learning paradigms that repeatedly drive early visual processing of transient signals can raise it. The evidence is graded: strongest for task-irrelevant coherent motion temporally paired with task targets, with one-year retention in a small subsample; weaker for contrast and dot-motion training; and, for flicker training, confined to amblyopic eyes starting below typical values. Three qualifications apply: samples are small; the motion and contrast paradigms were assessed with a small foveal stimulus on a macular pigment densitometer, whose equivalence with standard CFFF measurement is unestablished; and a minority of untrained controls show comparable changes. We examine whether the restriction originates at peripheral, thalamocortical, or cortical levels; available data do not adjudicate between them. Functional arguments for such a restriction are offered as rationales, not evidence. Proposed links to working-memory precision and metacognition are stated as predictions; first tests were largely negative.

papers.title: Open-Source Framework for the Visualization, Quantification, and Analysis of 4D Flow and High-Dimensional Magnetic Resonance Images
papers.summary: Background: Four-dimensional (4D) flow cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) captures 3D anatomy and blood velocity across the cardiac cycle, but current post-processing software is closed, varies across platforms, and sits outside open-source image-computing frameworks. We developed an open-source framework for the import, visualization, and quantification of 4D flow and other high-dimensional CMR within SlicerHeart, an extension for 3D Slicer. Methods: Import 4D Flow reads vendor DICOM, applies preprocessing, and stores velocities as a time-resolved vector field; Analyze 4D Flow provides measurement planes, streamline and Doppler-like visualization, segmentation propagation, and quantification. Underlying both, we extended the Insight Toolkit to store five- and higher-dimensional arrays. Flow quantification was compared with a commercial package (cvi42) and 2D phase contrast in 13 patients with congenital heart disease across 108 paired regions of interest (Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, ICCs). Consensus-recommended processing methods were also implemented as an open-source library with an automated test suite of analytic and CFD phantoms and clinical acquisitions. Results: The modules integrate with 3D Slicer's segmentation, registration, and rendering tools and export velocity fields and geometry for computational modeling. Agreement with cvi42 was close: forward volume bias -0.1 mL (95% limits of agreement 2.2 to -2.3; ICC 0.997), effective volume per minute bias -0.015 L/min (0.21 to -0.24; ICC 0.994). Against 2D phase contrast, forward volume bias (-2.2 mL) and mean absolute percentage error (21.8%) matched cvi42 (-2.1 mL; 21.3%). Conclusions: This open, extensible framework brings 4D flow CMR into an established image-computing ecosystem and agrees closely with a commercial reference; every step can be inspected, reproduced, and improved.

papers.title: A Closed-loop Framework to Discriminate Models Using Optimal Control
papers.summary: Predicting the response of an observed system to a known input is a fruitful first step to accurately control the system's dynamics. Despite the recent advances in fully data-driven algorithms, the most interpretable way to reach this goal is through mechanistic mathematical modeling. Here, we leverage optimal control and propose a closed-loop iterative method to choose among a set of candidate models the one that most accurately predicts an observed system. We assume that one has control over an input of the observed system and access to measurements of its response. Our approach is to identify the input control that maximally discriminates the response of the candidate models, allowing us to determine which model is best by comparing such responses with the observed data. We demonstrate our proposed framework in numerical simulations before applying it during an electrophysiology experiment, successfully discriminating between different models for photocurrents produced via opsin dynamics.

papers.title: Structural identifiability of partially-observed stochastic processes: from single-particle trajectories to total particle density data
papers.summary: The increasing availability of experimental data has intensified interest in calibrating stochastic models, raising fundamental questions about parameter identifiability. Structural identifiability determines whether parameters can be uniquely recovered from idealised data, a prerequisite to allow for parameter estimation in real-world scenarios. However, there is a lack of methodologies generally applicable to analyse the structural identifiability of such stochastic processes. Therefore, we develop a methodology for a class of spatio-temporal stochastic processes. We investigate how structural identifiability depends on the type of available data, distinguishing between single-particle trajectories and total particle density measurements. For trajectory data, we use a particle-based description that explicitly represents single-particle dynamics. For population-level data, we derive a partial differential equation representation, that describes the evolution of total particle density, and apply a differential algebra approach, common to ordinary differential equation analysis. We further introduce Taylor-series-expansion and Fourier-transform approaches to study the initial condition. We apply our methodology to an example model with a specified class of initial conditions. We show that the model is globally structurally identifiable given infinitely many, infinitely long single-particle trajectories, but only locally structurally identifiable from total particle density data, demonstrating that parameter identifiability depends on the type of data available.

papers.title: Finite-Element Electromagnetic Analysis and Evaluation of Antenna Performance Metrics Using a Quantum Linear System Solver
papers.summary: Electromagnetic analysis based on the finite element method is widely used in antenna design. At higher frequencies, however, the required mesh refinement makes solving large sparse linear systems the main contributor to computational cost. Quantum linear system solvers offer a potential means of accelerating this step, but their output is a superposition state: reconstructing all components of the classical solution vector would forfeit the quantum speedup. Prior studies have proposed methods for obtaining physical quantities such as scattering cross sections and scattering parameters from the solution state. To support antenna design using fault-tolerant quantum computers, we formulate the total radiated power, the radiated power within a prescribed solid angle, and the dielectric and conductive losses as observables for efficient evaluation from a quantum solution state. These observables avoid the measurement cost of reconstructing all components of the output quantum state. We develop an end-to-end hybrid quantum--classical workflow that combines finite-element electromagnetic analysis, matrix preconditioning, a quantum linear system solver, and the evaluation of antenna design metrics. To validate the workflow, we performed numerical experiments evaluating these observables for an axisymmetric coaxially fed monopole antenna. Under idealized conditions, the relative errors in the total radiated power and the dissipated power with respect to the classical finite-element solution were on the order of $10^{-3}$, confirming the consistency of the workflow. The proposed method is expected to provide a basis for using quantum linear system solvers to evaluate antenna performance and, in the future, to design high-frequency wireless devices.

papers.title: Finite-resource cooling of qudits beyond thermodynamic length
papers.summary: Cooling a quantum system with $N$ thermal machines costs more than Landauer's bound. For swap-based collision models the excess is set by thermodynamic length, which is optimal for qubits and was suggested by numerics to be optimal in general. We show that for qudits, permutations of energy eigenstates that use several resonant transitions at once do better for every spectrum, reducing the excess by up to 83% near the ground state. To second order, coherent collisions do no better, and at infinite temperature $d_M$-level machines reduce the excess by at most a factor $d_M-1$.

papers.title: Quantum manifestations of converse symmetry breaking
papers.summary: Quantum synchronization holds promise in advancing quantum technologies such as sensing, communication, and computation. A key challenge in this rapidly developing field is to identify mechanisms that can promote the emergence of synchronous dynamics. Here, we show that quantum synchronization can be enhanced by introducing controlled heterogeneity in the form of coupling mismatches. Using spin van der Pol oscillators as a model system, we show that this mechanism constitutes a quantum analog of the phenomenon of converse symmetry breaking previously identified in classical oscillator networks, where a synchronous state is stabilized by explicit symmetry breaking. We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.

papers.title: A Universal Approach to Hydrodynamics in Higher Dimensions via Tensor Networks
papers.summary: Extracting late-time hydrodynamic transport properties directly from microscopic quantum models, especially in dimensions beyond one, is believed to be classically intractable. This owes, in part, to the extensive growth of entanglement in higher dimensions and often a mismatch between geometric and tensor network locality. Here, we extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to accurately and quantitatively predict high-temperature transport coefficients (e.g. diffusion constants) in up to three dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to capture the slow crossover dynamics characteristic of weakly broken integrability. The intuition underlying our approach is to preserve the geometrically local information crucial for hydrodynamics throughout the time evolution, despite using a one-dimensional matrix product state ansatz for higher-dimensional calculations. Our work pushes the boundary of classical computability and opens the door to benchmarking the high-temperature, late-time dynamics of generic quantum simulators.

papers.title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
papers.summary: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and N\'eel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the N\'eel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The N\'eel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.

papers.title: Liouvillian spectral snapshots: A reduced-subspace approach for time-dependent and noisy open quantum systems
papers.summary: Driven-dissipative quantum devices are routinely operated with time-dependent drives and exposed to temporally correlated classical noise. When these perturbations vary on timescales comparable to the system's intrinsic dynamics, rotating-wave and Markovian approximations can fail, making effective static descriptions unreliable. As a result, accurately modeling systems in this regime often relies on simulating the full time-dependent master equation. This is particularly demanding for processes requiring long integration times, such as rare switching between metastable states, or for stochastic perturbations requiring averaging over many noise realizations. To address these challenges, we introduce Liouvillian spectral snapshots (LSS), a reduced-basis method that enables efficient simulation of such systems by projecting the master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace capturing their coarse-grained dynamics. LSS constructs this subspace by computing the slowly decaying, low-frequency eigenoperators of the Liouvillian at a few adaptively sampled perturbation values and compressing them into a common basis. This basis is built once and can be reused across noise realizations and perturbation parameters, reducing the cost of ensemble averages and parameter sweeps.

papers.title: Beyond the Kubo formula: unification of adiabatic and isothermal response in quantum systems
papers.summary: The static limit of the Kubo susceptibility describes the adiabatic response of an isolated quantum system, in which energy-level occupations remain unchanged, and generally differs from the isothermal susceptibility, where these occupations readjust to thermal equilibrium. In this work, we introduce a single dynamical framework in which the adiabatic and isothermal responses arise naturally as two distinct limiting regimes. This can be done by considering explicitly an open system version of the Kubo approach in which the dissipation is governed by a typical thermalization rate of the system. By exchanging the order of the static limit and of the vanishing thermalization rate limit, the protocol yields either the adiabatic or isothermal response. This protocol has a solid physical motivation in terms of the thermalization dynamics and is valid for generic systems. We apply it to the case of the magnetic response of the electron gas and reproduce the expected results.

papers.title: Witnessing and quantifying stellar rank with the Wigner function
papers.summary: Quantifying non-Gaussianity is essential for assessing the computational power of bosonic quantum systems. We introduce a framework to witness and quantify non-Gaussianity from displaced parity measurements, and we directly apply it to experimental data obtained with superconducting cavities. Our method estimates fidelities with target pure states from the displaced parity measurements, enabling certification of non-Gaussianity via the stellar rank. We further introduce refined witnesses computed by measuring the value of the Wigner function at a few points, providing efficient certification tools outperforming existing ones. Applying these techniques to Fock, binomial, cat, and GKP experimental data, we rigorously certify non-Gaussian resources and establish a stellar rank of $8$ for a GKP state, setting a new benchmark across all quantum platforms. Our methods enable a rigorous quantification of non-Gaussian quantum resources directly applicable to superconducting devices.

papers.title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
papers.summary: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

papers.title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
papers.summary: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.

papers.title: Hypergraph cycle enumeration for efficient inference of planted k-XOR with smooth trade-off
papers.summary: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.

papers.title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks
papers.summary: Variational quantum algorithms leave the durations of Hamiltonian evolutions open for a classical optimizer to set. We present VHamilton, a minimal extension of the Hamilton quantum programming language in which such durations are open clocks: one program denotes a family of Hamiltonian trajectories, and a valuation fills its clocks with exact dyadic times, so that each instance is an ordinary Hamilton program that compiles to circuits as before. Because the semantics stays exact and affine in the clocks, the Hamiltonian structure of a variational program remainsavail able for reasoning about every valuation at once. Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.

papers.title: Preparation of a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator on a superconducting quantum processor
papers.summary: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states, hosting topological order and fractionalized anyonic excitations. Their realization poses a demanding target for quantum simulation. Here, we realize a bosonic FCI on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor using classically optimized variational circuits. We target a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus, eliminating physical edges and providing a favorable geometry for accessing fractional quantum Hall physics in a small system. On a $4\times4$ qubit lattice, we prepare both the four-boson FCI ground state and a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. Measurements of particle densities and correlations reproduce the characteristic structure of the target states, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes. The preparation of these strongly correlated topological states with shallow circuits establishes a route toward the digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations, including measurements of topological invariants and anyonic braiding.

papers.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
papers.summary: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

papers.title: Entangled Measurement Outcomes for Optimal Postselection in Quantum Batteries
papers.summary: Postselection can enhance the performance of a selected quantum battery branch, raising the question of whether the optimum can always be achieved by product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems. For battery auxiliary states obtained by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy reduces to a generalized Rayleigh quotient. For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum if and only if the eigenspace associated with the largest generalized eigenvalue contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap therefore occurs precisely when this eigenspace is one dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector. Noisy W and GHZ states display qualitatively different behavior: the three qubit W state exhibits a strict gap throughout 0<p<1, whereas the three qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as the coupling strength is varied. By contrast, the outcome averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, showing that the joint measurement advantage is genuinely postselective.

papers.title: Probing Operator Spreading with Local Quantum Fluctuations
papers.summary: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally challenging, often requiring effective reversal of many-body dynamics. Here, we propose an alternative approach to probing operator spreading through local quantum fluctuations, using only forward evolution and local measurements. Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, we introduce a differential local variance and establish a rigorous bound connecting it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, we derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. In integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs reveal qualitatively consistent propagation fronts. Our results establish local quantum fluctuations as an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading.

papers.title: Anomalous superradiant phases in a quantum Rabi zigzag chain under a synthetic gauge field
papers.summary: We present the phase diagram of a one-dimensional quantum Rabi zigzag chain under an artificial gauge field, which is implemented via phase-modulated next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) hopping. For a system size of $N=8$, we analytically determine the order parameters and critical thresholds, identifying five distinct superradiant phases. For strong nearest-neighbor (NN) coupling, the system exhibits either a ferro-superradiant (FSR) or an antiferro-superradiant (AFSR) phase depending on its sign. Increasing NNN coupling induces a stripe antiferro-superradiant (sAFSR) phase with antiparallel NNN and parallel NN displacements, which is distinct from the conventional AFSR phase. Tuning the magnetic flux drives the system into chiral or antichiral superradiant phases with opposite ground-state photon currents, which are different from the conventional superradiant phases. Remarkably, geometric frustration within each triangular plaquette stabilizes chiral phases even at small magnetic flux while suppressing the sAFSR phase, which vanishes for $N=6$. Mapping the system onto an effective magnetic Hamiltonian yields an analogous phase diagram featuring distinct magnetic phases, offering insight into the anomalous superradiant phases. This equivalence establishes a quantum optical platform for simulating chiral magnetism.

papers.title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control
papers.summary: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $\Lambda$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.

papers.title: Testing hardware quantum machine learning claims with a null circuit: fill prediction on Binance futures with 129 qubits of an IBM Heron processor
papers.summary: Quantum processors are now used as feature generators for classical models on tabular data. A circuit encodes each record, the device returns expectation values, and a classical model learns from them. A recent report claimed large gains from such features, gains that appeared only on noisy hardware. These claims are hard to check, because a quantum device is not a static function. Its state changes from job to job and from one calibration to the next, and that drift can leak information about the outcome into the features. We propose a five-step protocol for testing claims of this kind. It runs a circuit that carries no data in the same jobs as the real one. It checks whether the hardware leaves a recognizable mark on each job. It compares random and natural assignments of records to jobs, replays the null results under other submission orders, and closes the leak with a job-purged backtest. We apply it, pre-registered, to the HSBC and IBM study of fill probabilities in bond trading, which reported a large hardware-only gain. We use a public analog task and run the study's circuit on a 129-qubit chain of an IBM Heron processor. Under controlled assignment the hardware features give no gain over classical features, and the device reproduces the ideal features about as well as shot noise allows. Yet every job carries a distinct fingerprint. A circuit with no data at all predicts fills well above chance when records are batched by outcome and the same job sits on both sides of the train/test split. Removing that overlap removes the effect. The protocol costs under an hour of processor time and is designed for any hardware feature or kernel pipeline on tabular data.

papers.title: Optimality of the Petz-Fuchs Smoothed State
papers.summary: Quantum state smoothing is an estimation technique that uses past and future measurement information obtained from a continuous-in-time measurement record to reconstruct the state of an open quantum system. Recently, there has been a new approach to quantum state smoothing based on quantum retrodiction known as the Petz-Fuchs smoothed state. Here I prove that this Petz-Fuchs smoothed state majorizes all other smoothed states that only depend on the filtered state (the operator conditioned on the past measurement record) and the retrofiltered effect (the operator describing the future measurement record). To do this, I characterize the set of all possible smoothed states satisfying this condition.

papers.title: PyQLAS: A Quantum-Classical Hybrid Solver Library for Linear Systems
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms solve a linear system at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically in its dimension, but on present-day hardware that advantage is realised only if the quantum and the classical parts of a solve are apportioned deliberately. We present PyQLAS, a quantum--classical hybrid library for linear systems that exposes this apportionment as a design parameter rather than a fixed assumption. PyQLAS builds three nested solvers around a single variational core---a variational solver, an outer residual iteration, and a Krylov-subspace projection---so that the quantum subroutine can be held at a fixed circuit width while the classical host absorbs the growth of the problem. Around them, the library supplies preconditioning at two independent levels, dimension alignment, checkpointing, and device-budget control, and a solve written against the interface runs unchanged on an exact state-vector simulator, on a local sampler, and on a real superconducting processor. The library is validated on the IEEE 118-bus power flow, a standard test system in which the linear solver is embedded in a classical Newton iteration. There, the iteration converges to the specified tolerance and reproduces the classical reference solution to within $2.3\times10^{-8}$ p.u.\ in voltage magnitude and $3.4\times10^{-6}$ degrees in voltage angle.

papers.title: Time-Domain Multiplexing for Resource-Efficient Heralded GKP State Preparation
papers.summary: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are key resources for fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing, but their conditional preparation via Gaussian boson sampling involves a trade-off between source count and photon-number resolution. Distributing heralding photons across more measured modes reduces the resolution required per mode, yet increases the number of simultaneously operated squeezed sources in fully squeezed spatial architectures. Here, we show that time-domain multiplexing (TDM) can reduce these physical source requirements while preserving GKP state quality. Using an end-to-end differentiable Bargmann framework, we find that TDM circuits reusing one or two squeezed sources achieve fidelities comparable to fully squeezed spatial circuits across several configurations. Selected nine-mode configurations retain fidelities above 0.95 with one photon heralded in each measured mode, mitigating detector resolution demands without a proportional increase in source count. Loss-aware reoptimization further shows that, under the investigated spatial loss models, two-mode TDM maintains fidelities near 0.80 at 1.0 dB per channel, whereas the corresponding spatial benchmarks fall below 0.60. These results demonstrate that temporal reuse provides an effective architectural route for balancing source overhead, detection demands, and state preparation performance in the presence of optical loss.

papers.title: Loss-aware optimization of realistic GKP gid states
papers.summary: Realistic preparation of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states, the prime candidates for quantum computation with bosonic systems, is inevitably burdened by photon loss. We show how taking this loss into account can lead to more robust quantum states, thereby diminishing its negative influence. Using GKP squeezing as an operational figure of merit, we formulate a loss-aware optimization procedure based on the ground state representation of GKP states. Numerical simulations for square, hexagonal, and asymmetric GKP states show that the optimal preparation generally requires a different initial grid spacing than that of the desired ideal code state. For symmetric and hexagonal lattices, the optimal parameters asymptotically follow the simple scaling relation. The optimized states exhibit better GKP squeezing and greater resilience to losses. These results provide a simple and experimentally relevant strategy for improving realistic photonic GKP state preparation in the presence of known photon loss.

papers.title: Helper-assisted quantum sensing with low dressed-state leakage
papers.summary: We study a two-qubit sensing protocol in which only a helper qubit is read out. Calibrated loading and unloading encode a transverse signal in the helper's phase, keep leakage out of a selected dressed-state band small, and return the sensor close to its idle ground state. We derive an information bound for a single sensor whose excitation stays below a prescribed budget, and simulate repeated operation with an uncertain coupling and finite-duration resets in a driven open-system model. At the tested settings, finite measurement records support estimation with infrequent resets. A helper flip at zero coupling, combined with a reversal of the coupling sign, suppresses a static helper offset shared across a record while retaining the signal, at a cost of about 27% of the no-offset information of a plain sequence of equal duration. Under slowly varying noise, averaging each cycle's likelihood over the correct noise law removes most of the added bias, and a wrong noise law can worsen the estimate. A selected directly read sensor with ideal controls and repeated nondemolition verification has the higher information rate. Any practical benefit of avoiding direct readout therefore requires a device-specific disturbance model.

papers.title: Analytic level statistics of the quantum Rabi model
papers.summary: We derive an analytic expression for the distribution of level spacings in the quantum Rabi model. At high energies, the spectrum in a fixed parity sector takes the asymptotic form of a uniformly spaced ladder modulated by a decaying oscillation. The alternating sign of this oscillation separates successive spacings into two branches. For a finite window containing many oscillations, counting how often the two branches exceed a given spacing yields an analytic expression for the spacing density at leading order. The oscillation amplitude at the lower end of the window sets the range of spacings, and its value at the upper end fixes the positions of two cusps that form twin peaks. Spacing histograms from exact diagonalization agree with the analytic density, including its spacing range and twin peak positions. At leading order, the same spectral analysis also yields an expression for the ratio of consecutive spacings, a statistic that requires no spectral unfolding. The resulting ratio statistics agree closely with those from exact diagonalization. For windows that continue to contain many oscillations, the spacing and ratio peaks move toward unity at higher energies as the spectrum approaches a uniformly spaced ladder. The same counting approach can be explored in other systems with controlled spectral asymptotics, slowly varying spacing branches, and windows containing many oscillations.

papers.title: oracq: A Modular Framework for Implementing and Analyzing Quantum Scientific Computing Algorithms
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms for scientific computing are specified against access models such as block-encodings, sparse oracles, state preparations, and quantum random-access memories. Their concrete realization is deliberately left open, yet it is a research variable that changes both the numerical behavior and the resource cost of the program, so every reported conclusion is attributable to one realization. In this paper, we present oracq, a Python framework that makes this choice a managed and checkable decision. Our claim is linguistic rather than infrastructural. Algorithms are stored as persistent register-level programs whose oracle slots are declared and typed but unimplemented. A separate binding pass links compatible realizations, so one stored algorithm can be re-bound to a gate network, a QRAM-backed table, or compiled reversible arithmetic and compared across them. Typed QRAM resources, a compiler from pure Python numerical formulas to reversible fixed-point circuits, and block-encoding algebra with qubitization and QSVT-style kernels supply the constructions. Two end-to-end workflows exercise the framework, a quantum finite-volume pipeline for the compressible Euler equations and a quantum homotopy-analysis pipeline that lifts nonlinear PDEs to composable linear input models. The verification methodology separates implementation error from method error, and logical resource accounts cover programs before and after binding. The framework is openly available at https://github.com/IAI-USTC-Quantum/oracq.

papers.title: Almost-Quantum Correlations Violate Information Causality
papers.summary: Information causality (IC) posits that communicating m classical bits cannot give the receiver access to more than m bits of information about the sender's independent data. Although IC holds in quantum theory and excludes a broad class of supra-quantum correlations, its validity for the almost-quantum set has remained open. This semidefinite relaxation of the quantum set satisfies nontrivial communication complexity, no advantage for non-local computation, macroscopic locality, local orthogonality, and numerical evidence has suggested that it may also satisfy IC. Here we show that almost-quantum correlations violate IC, and do so without bound. Unlike earlier violations of IC, which rely on biased guesses, ours is driven by zero-error certificates: each is rare but never wrong, carries information linear in its probability, and vouches for many of the sender's bits at once. This establishes a sharp dichotomy: either IC is a valid physical principle that excludes these correlations, or any nonsignalling theory realizing them admits no mutual information obeying consistency, data processing and the chain rule. In the latter case, we discuss why the chain rule is the natural property to relinquish, and how this possibility relates to histories-based formulations and to locality defined relative to the state rather than presupposed in a fixed spacetime.

papers.title: An Unbounded Separation of Almost-Quantum and Commuting-Operator Correlations in Zero-Error Communication
papers.summary: Almost-quantum correlations form the $\mathtt{1+AB}$ level of the Navascu\'es--Pironio--Ac\'in hierarchy. They strictly contain the quantum set, are characterized by a single semidefinite program, arise in Sorkin's quantum measure theory, and satisfy several principles proposed to single out quantum theory. We show that they are nevertheless unboundedly stronger than quantum correlations in a zero-error communication task. Alice and Bob receive labels $s,t\in[N]$, $N\ge3$; after one bit from Alice, Bob must decide whether $s=t$, never erring but allowed to abstain. For every model of quantum correlations, from finite-dimensional tensor products to commuting operators, the optimal worst-case probability of a conclusive answer is exactly $1/N$, the value attained with shared randomness, so the bound does not depend on the resolution of Tsirelson's problem. An explicit family of almost-quantum correlations attains $1/19$ for every $N$. For certificates of equality from binary-outcome boxes, we solve the underlying semidefinite programs in closed form. The almost-quantum optimum equals $N^2/(17N^2-80N+64)$ for $N\ge8$ and tends to $1/17$. The first level of the hierarchy, which coincides with the set singled out by macroscopic locality, attains $N/[8(N-2)]$, which tends to $1/8$; its optimal boxes lie outside the almost-quantum set for every $N\ge5$. For longer messages, entanglement saves at most one bit over shared randomness, whereas almost-quantum correlations reduce the one-way zero-error cost of deciding equality of $n$-bit strings from $n$ bits to at most $13$. The quantum bound also yields a linear witness of post-quantumness on a face of the nonsignalling polytope.

papers.title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction
papers.summary: We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

papers.title: Symmetries and model reduction in a $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit
papers.summary: Engineered symmetries in superconducting circuits can protect quantum information; much like selection rules in atomic physics, they forbid transitions between the qubit states. Protected circuits, however, combine several loops and islands and host multiple nonlinearly coupled modes, calling for reduced low-energy models that inherit the circuit symmetries and make the protection manifest. We develop such a reduction for the $\cos 2\varphi$ transmon qubit, recently realized experimentally with a two-Cooper-pair interferometer, whose circuit hosts three coupled modes. Exploiting the separation of energy scales between the heavy transmon mode and the light internal modes of the interferometer, we derive an effective single-band Born-Oppenheimer model, including its geometric correction, and extend it to several bands. We identify the symmetries of the full and reduced Hamiltonians and derive exact selection rules. Finally, we identify a parameter regime beyond the single-band description that suppresses flux-noise dephasing without degrading charge-noise protection.

For any continuous multivariate function, the joint quantum state converges uniformly to the target output register, linking classical superposition theory with probabilistic and coherent quantum circuits.

papers.title: Windowed Catodyne Measurements: Continuum Approximation versus Exact Discrete Photon-Number Treatment
papers.summary: We analyze a family of measurements obtained by retaining only a finite window of the photon-sum variable in catodyne detection, where a Schr\"odinger cat state serves as the local oscillator. In the continuum approximation, the window half-width appears to act as a continuous knob for coherence. However, a treatment on the discrete photon-number lattice shows that, in the strong-LO regime, the coherence conditioned on the difference outcome is not suppressed by the window. The exact parity-sensitive success probability is a staircase function of and , whose plateau structure and magnitude the continuum formulas fail to capture, especially for small and narrow windows. For remote preparation of cat states, an exact calculation with a finitely squeezed resource shows that the remote state keeps a purity close to one when x is resolved, and loses purity mainly when x is not recorded. papers.title: Quantum machine learning geospatial time-series by seasonal encoding
papers.summary: Quantum data reuploading models can increase the expressive capacity of variational quantum models, but do not necessarily improve predictive performance. In the present work, we investigate this behavior for seasonal time series forecasting and show that data encoding determines how well temporal structures are represented as circuit depth increases. We develop a fidelity-based quantum geometric description in which repeated encodings contribute to an effective input generator, so that reuploading depth changes the quantum geometry through which approximately recurrent inputs are distinguished. We construct fixed and adaptive seasonal encodings that represent observation magnitude and seasonal phase in distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates. We evaluate these encodings for monthly precipitation derived from ERA5-Land, a global reanalysis dataset, from a representative semi-arid, drought-prone tropical region in East Africa, using a 14-month lag window and reuploading depths $L$= 1-6. We find that in ideal simulations, standard value-based encodings degrade markedly with depth, whereas adaptive seasonal encodings preserve temporal correlation, spectral structure, and forecasting accuracy. Noisy simulations show that this encoding hierarchy persists at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are limited by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with established classical forecasting methods (ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs). These results identify structure-aware quantum data encoding as a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models.
